messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell slows a step before the others, letting Bram's bulk take the front of the track. His eyes aren't on the man in the doorway yet — they go to the sheds, the spoil heaps, the lifting frame, the half-loaded cart with no mule.*

*Low, without turning his head:* "Tools down where they were working. Cart left mid-load. Nobody walks off a wage like that for lunch." *A beat.* "Bram, you do the talking — you've the face for it. I'll keep my eyes on the sheds. Sefa, stay between us, aye?"

*He keeps his hands loose and visible, nowhere near the shortsword, and lets his gaze drift over the yard as they come on — doorways of the sheds, the shadow under the lifting frame, the ground near the lower cut: footprints, drag marks, blood, anything that says where the quarrymen went and whether they went willingly.*

*To the warden, pitched friendly and plain, once they're near enough:* "Morning. Maela Thorn sent us for the case. Quiet day?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Quiet for a working quarry,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa.

I approach the house at an easy walk, sword sheathed and shield held low, watching the sheds and lower cut as I cross the yard. I stop a few paces from the man, giving him room.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us to collect her sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I glance back at the abandoned cart. “Everyone stopped for something?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa slows as the silence settles over the yard, one hand drifting to the book at her belt without quite touching it. She glances to Pell and Bram.

"That must be the warden, but a whole quarry gone still? No mules, no men, just him watching us." She keeps her voice low. "I'll say a word to him from here. If I'm wrong, we've lost nothing. If you see anything move behind those sheds, sing out."

She steps forward a few paces, not enough to close the distance, and raises a hand in greeting that could be friendly or a signal to stop.

"Morning!" she calls, clear and even. "Maela Thorn sent us from Beregost. We're expected — for a case of dye-salts from the warden. Is that you?"

scenes.narration:
Bram walks up the track in front at an easy pace, shield low. Sefa stays a few steps back between the two men. Pell drifts to one side, and his eyes go over the yard the way they'd go over a merchant's back wall.

Close up, the quarry is just as quiet. White dust lies over everything in a soft skin, and it keeps every mark made on it. Pell reads the ground near the lower cut, the shadow under the lifting frame, the stretch between the sheds and the cart.

Pell sees it well enough. Nobody was dragged off anywhere. There's no blood, no scuffle, no furrow of heels in the dust. A crowd of boot prints, a dozen men or a few more, heads down the cart track the way the three of them just came. The strides are short and even, overlapping, the tracks of men walking together and in no hurry. One set of mule hooves goes with them, led on a short line. The edges of the prints have gone soft under a night's settling dust. They were made yesterday, not this morning.

The tools aren't scattered either. Seen from this angle, the hammers by the lower cut lie in a row along a squared block, heads together. The wedges are stacked beside them and every handle points at the warden's house. The cart's traces were unbuckled, not cut. Someone laid all this out on purpose, the way you'd put a key on a table before walking out a door.

The man in the doorway lets them come. Bram stops a few paces off, Sefa's call carries across the yard, and Pell's easy question lands last. The warden looks at each of them in turn, the big one first. Up close he's in his fifties, grey-bearded, with white dust in the creases of his knuckles and his apron. The keys at his belt are old iron, a dozen of them.

"Hale. Osric Hale. I'm the warden." His voice is gravel, and he uses no more of it than he has to. He tips his chin at the cart. "They stopped for pay. Noon bell, yesterday. Three weeks of none, and they walked." He doesn't sound angry about it. "I'd have walked too, if it was my back."

Then he looks at Sefa, because she named the salts. "The case is inside. Sealed, like she wants it." He doesn't step out of the doorway. "Thorn's bought it. So she's paid someone. Not me, and not them." He nods at the empty track. "Before it leaves my house, I'll hear who she paid. And whether she knows where my men's wages went."

He waits with his arms folded, his eyes on Bram, as if the big man in mail is the one who'll answer for all three.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I nod. “Three weeks unpaid is reason enough to stop. I’ve left a wagon standing for less.”

I keep my hands away from my sword. “But we’re hired carriers, Hale. Thorn told us to fetch a sealed case from you and bring it back by sunset. She didn’t tell us who took her money, or that your men were owed.”

“Who handles the wages here—and who sold her the salts? If you’ve a tally or a letter she needs to answer for, we can carry that too. I won’t promise an answer I haven’t got.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her hands open at her sides, meeting the warden's eyes without challenge.

"She paid us, Warden — ninety gold to walk the road and carry the case, and not one coin of it until it's in her shop by sunset. That's the whole of what we know. If your men's wages have gone missing, we hadn't heard a word of it until now."

She lets that settle, then adds, calm: "Let us take what's under her seal, and we'll carry your complaint straight back to her. Or keep us here, and she'll say the case never came and owe us nothing. Either way, you'll have no answer."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell lets the yard go and drifts back toward Bram's shoulder. Low, for his two companions:* "Tracks say the same as he does. A dozen men, one mule, walked down the road yesterday noon, easy stride, nobody chasing. Tools laid out neat as a note. He's not lying about that much."

*Then he squares up to Hale — not crowding him, just stepping in so the warden has to look at him too and not only at the mail.*

"Hale. Fair question, so here's a fair answer. We're hired hands. Thorn pays us ninety on delivery and not a copper before. What she paid for the salts, or who to, she didn't say and we didn't ask — which is our fault, not yours." *A small shrug.* "But I grew up watching money move, and it doesn't move to a warden with a dozen keys and no men. Who owns Whitestone? Because whoever that is took Thorn's coin, and it never came back up this road. That's who's holding your wages — not her, not us."

*He glances at the empty cart, then back.*

"Here's what I can offer. Give me the owner's name and I'll put it to Thorn's face tonight, in front of her buyer if you like — merchants hate that. Write it down if you want it in your own words; I'll carry the letter with the case and bring you her answer or her silence. And I'll say this plain, because you'd rather hear it plain: if the case isn't in Beregost by sunset, nobody gets paid at all. Not us, not you, and not the men who walked. The only coin on this hill is in that box, and it only turns into wages if it moves."

*He watches the warden's face while he talks — the eyes, the hands near the keys, whether he's a man holding out for leverage or a man who's just tired and wants someone to notice.*

scenes.narration:
Osric hears all three of them out without moving. He listens to Bram first, then to Sefa's ninety gold and her "either way", then to Pell, who steps in close enough that the warden has to look at him too and not only at the mail.

Pell watches the man's face while he talks, and there's not much in it to puzzle over. Osric's hands stay folded and never go near the keys. When Sefa says *keep us here*, his jaw shifts, the look of a man told something he already knew. This isn't a man playing for leverage. He's spent three weeks writing letters, and these are the first people up the track to give him a straight answer. Once, when Pell says *the only coin on this hill*, the warden's eyes go past them toward the lower cut and come straight back. That's all.

"House Vandarren," Osric says. "Patriars, in the Gate. Whitestone's theirs on paper. Their factor's a man called Tull, in the Lower City. Coin comes up from Tull, I pay the lads. That's how it's gone for thirty years." He tips his head at the empty track. "Three weeks back it stopped coming. I wrote four times. Nothing."

He looks at Bram. "You asked who sold her the salts. Not me. I cut it, I box it, I seal it, it goes. Somebody paid for it, and that's Tull, so that's Vandarren." He breathes out through his nose. "Fourteen men, three weeks. Fifty-odd gold, and the carter's owed more than the rest. They're in Beregost now, drinking what they had left. Not taken, not run off. Walked. They'll tell anyone who stands them a round."

For a moment he doesn't say anything. Then he unfolds his arms and steps back out of the doorway.

"Come in. Case is on the table."

The house is one long room, cool after the glare. There's a hearth with a kettle on a hook, a cot, shelves of ledgers swollen with damp, and white dust everywhere, even here. On a plank table under the window sits a case about the size of a bread loaf. It's oak with iron corners, bound with waxed cord, and a disc of red wax on the knot carries Maela Thorn's mark. Beside it lie a pen, an ink-pot gone thick, and a sheet of paper with three lines on it in a big, cramped hand, two of them crossed out.

Osric stands by the table and doesn't sit. "It goes with you. And a letter goes with it, to Thorn. She'll know what her money bought, and she can ask Tull where the rest went. She's a buyer, so he'll answer her." He looks at the crossed-out lines, then at Sefa, since she spoke for the money. "I cut stone. I don't write much." He pushes the pen an inch across the plank toward her. "You write a fair hand?"

The case sits on the table between them. Nobody has touched it yet.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa crosses to the table without touching the case, turning the sheet so she can read the warden's crossed-out attempts.

"I can. Write, I mean." She picks up the pen, tests the nib lightly on the edge of the ink-pot, and looks to Osric. "Give me your words, and I'll set them down plain. Short so it can't be waved off."

She lets him dictate. When he mentions Tull or Vandarren, she takes care to spell the names right, asking once and repeating them back. As she finishes, she glances over the lines and says, not unkindly: "If you'll allow me, I'll put at the end that the quarry stands silent and the men are in Beregost unpaid. That tells her what's waiting if the coin doesn't come. It's the truth, and it'll be heard."

She doesn't sign anything in her own name unless the warden asks — it's his letter. She writes slowly and cleanly, the same kind of steady hand she once used dyeing labels for the hospice.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell nods at Sefa when the pen slides her way — she'll have the cleaner hand of the three — and goes to the table himself. He doesn't lift the case yet. He looks it over first: the cord, the knot, the wax disc, the iron corners. Then he tilts it an inch to feel the weight settle, and sets it down exactly where it was.*

*Over his shoulder, to Osric, easy:* "Mind if I check the seal's whole? Not doubting you — doubting the road. If Thorn says it was opened, I want to know it was whole when it left your table, and I want you to have watched me look."

*While Sefa writes, he catches the warden's eye and keeps his voice low, as if it's nothing.* "Something else. When I said the only coin on this hill was in that box, you looked at the lower cut. Twice now. Is there something down there I ought to know about before we walk off with Vandarren's property? A second case, a strongbox, a Tull's man who didn't leave with the others?" *He spreads his hands.* "Not asking to take it. Asking so I'm not surprised on the road."

*Then, to the others, glancing at the light through the window:* "We've got the half-day back and the sun won't wait on a letter. Sefa, keep it short — the name Tull, the sum, three weeks, fourteen men — he can sign it. Bram, you'll want to carry the case; nobody tries their luck with the man in mail. I'll take the back on the road."

*He pauses at the door of his own thought and adds, to Osric:* "Your lads are drinking in Beregost tonight. If Thorn gives me her answer, where do I find them — which tavern?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“We’ll put the letter in her hands with the case,” I tell Osric. “Your men’s wages ought to be in it, not our guess at where they went.”

I leave the pen for Sefa and look over the case’s cord, wax and corners without disturbing the seal, checking for damage before I take charge of it.

“Anything we need to know about carrying these salts—keep them upright, keep them dry?” I ask. “And if Thorn has an answer for you, where in Beregost will we find your carter?”

scenes.narration:
Sefa turns the sheet toward her. The warden's three lines are written in a big, cramped hand pressed hard into the paper. The first reads *To Mistress Thorn*. The second, crossed out, reads *The salt is paid for and my men are not*. The third, also crossed out, gets as far as *I have wrote to Tull four* and stops where the nib split.

Osric watches her test the nib. He thinks about it before he speaks, then gives her his words one at a time, like setting stones.

"To Mistress Thorn. The salt you bought is cut and sealed and sent." He waits for the pen. "You paid Tull. Tull is House Vandarren's factor in the Gate. None of that coin came to Whitestone." When she asks how to spell it, he says "Tull. Two l's," and when she reads it back, "Vandarren. Like the mark on the deeds." He goes on. "Fourteen men, three weeks unpaid. Fifty gold and some. The carter's owed most. I have written to Tull four times. No answer. Ask him where it went. He'll answer a buyer." He stops there, as if he's used up what he had.

Sefa offers her last line. He looks at the sheet, not at her. "Put it." She writes that the quarry stands silent and the men are in Beregost, unpaid. When she turns the paper to him, he takes the pen in his fist like a chisel and signs *O. Hale, Warden*, so hard the ink pools in the last stroke. He blows on it, folds it twice with his thumbnail and puts it in Sefa's hand. "Your hand wrote it. You give it to her."

Meanwhile Pell asks about the seal, and Osric lifts one shoulder. "Look." He stands there while Pell does. Pell goes over the case the way he'd go over a lock. The waxed cord is wound tight and even, with no slack at the knot. The wax disc is whole, its edge unbroken, Maela's mark crisp, and there's no warm-knife smear where someone might have lifted it and laid it back. The iron corners are nailed true. When he tilts it, the weight inside shifts a little, like dry grit in a packed box, then settles. Bram looks it over after him and finds the same: a sound case that nobody has opened since it was tied. Then he takes it in hand. It's heavier than a loaf, lighter than a stone, and it carries easily under his shield arm.

"Keep it dry," Osric tells Bram. "Damp, it cakes. Dry, it keeps." He thinks. "That's all I know of carrying it. It's not my trade past the box."

Pell drops his voice and asks about the lower cut. Osric's eyes don't go there this time. He keeps them on Pell, which takes him some effort.

"No strongbox. Nobody of Tull's. Nobody at all." Then, slower: "The salt comes from down there. Old workings below the lower cut, flooded since before my time. It grows on the walls like frost, rose-white. We scrape it from a ledge." He breathes out. "The ground's hollow under half this hill. Old galleries, old floors. Some of it's rotten. Keep to the track, and don't go poking at the low end."

He doesn't say anything after that. Pell hears more behind it, the way you hear a room on the far side of a door. It isn't a lie about a strongbox. It's something the man has decided not to put into words, and he stands very still while he doesn't.

Then come the questions about the men. Both Pell and Bram asked, and Osric answers them together. "The Red Sheaf. Low end of Beregost, past the smithies. Cheapest ale on the Way." He tips his chin at the letter in Sefa's hand. "Carter's Hob Carrow. Red beard, one mule, a temper. If Thorn sends anything, give it to Hob. He'll share it out straight. He can't count crooked."

He looks round the three of them, at the case under Bram's arm and the letter in Sefa's hand, and something in his shoulders loosens a little.

"That's it, then. Track's the same one you came up."

The sun through the window has climbed past the frame. You have a half-day of road ahead of you, and the day is still on your side, with time in hand before sunset.

 (Out of game: no roll was needed for any of the three. Sefa writing a letter and Pell checking a seal are routine work in their own trades. Pell's question was answered in the scene: no strongbox, nobody of Tull's, the salt comes from down there. What Osric chose to hold back is his own decision, and asking someone a question isn't a check. If Pell wants to read what the warden is keeping back, his player can say so and that's an Insight roll.)

- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell doesn't push. He lets the silence sit a breath longer than is comfortable, then gives Osric a small nod — the kind that says* I heard what you didn't say *— and leaves it on the table where the case was.*

"Keep to the track. Fair enough." *He lets it go, then can't quite, and adds lightly:* "If that hollow ground ever starts saying things you don't like, Hale, the Red Sheaf isn't the only place a man can send word. Thorn's shop will know where to find us for a few days."

*To the others, already moving for the door:* "Right. Bram, the case stays dry and stays with you — if we meet anyone on the road, you keep walking and let me and Sefa do the stopping. Sefa, the letter's yours till it's in Thorn's hand. I'll hang back thirty paces and watch our dust. If I whistle twice, that's trouble behind; once, I'm just bored."

*At the threshold he pauses and looks back at the warden.* "Hob Carrow, red beard, can't count crooked. I'll remember. Thanks for the straight answer — there's not many of those on this coast."

*Then he's out into the glare, eyes already on the track where the quarrymen's prints lead down, checking whether any newer marks have come up it since dawn.*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Hob Carrow, Red Sheaf. Understood.” I settle the case securely in my pack, wrapped in my bedroll against knocks. “Thank you, Hale. Mind yourself up here.”

Outside, I glance at the sky and check the pack’s flap covers the case before setting off along the track toward Beregost.

“I’ll take the front. Pell, give a word if anything follows us.” I keep an easy, steady road pace—no lingering, but no wearing ourselves out while we have daylight to spare.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa tucks Osric's letter into a pouch at her belt, not into the Book of Shadows — paper and wards don't mix, and this letter is owed to Thorn, not to the Lantern.

"We'll see this into her hands, and your words with it." She meets Osric's eyes. "If we find Hob Carrow, we'll tell him what you said about the sharing."

Then she turns to Pell and Bram, settling her pack and moving toward the door.

"Case to Thorn before we do anything else. After that, if the road's been kind, the Red Sheaf for Hob — but not at the cost of the sunset."

(Round 4 — one paragraph per character in this scene.)

Pell Dunmore: *Pell doesn't push. He lets the silence sit a breath longer than is comfortable, then gives Osric a small nod — the kind that says* I heard what you didn't say *— and leaves it on the table where the case was.*

"Keep to the track. Fair enough." *He lets it go, then can't quite, and adds lightly:* "If that hollow ground ever starts saying things you don't like, Hale, the Red Sheaf isn't the only place a man can send word. Thorn's shop will know where to find us for a few days."

*To the others, already moving for the door:* "Right. Bram, the case stays dry and stays with you — if we meet anyone on the road, you keep walking and let me and Sefa do the stopping. Sefa, the letter's yours till it's in Thorn's hand. I'll hang back thirty paces and watch our dust. If I whistle twice, that's trouble behind; once, I'm just bored."

*At the threshold he pauses and looks back at the warden.* "Hob Carrow, red beard, can't count crooked. I'll remember. Thanks for the straight answer — there's not many of those on this coast."

*Then he's out into the glare, eyes already on the track where the quarrymen's prints lead down, checking whether any newer marks have come up it since dawn.*

Bram Halloway: “Hob Carrow, Red Sheaf. Understood.” I settle the case securely in my pack, wrapped in my bedroll against knocks. “Thank you, Hale. Mind yourself up here.”

Outside, I glance at the sky and check the pack’s flap covers the case before setting off along the track toward Beregost.

“I’ll take the front. Pell, give a word if anything follows us.” I keep an easy, steady road pace—no lingering, but no wearing ourselves out while we have daylight to spare.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa tucks Osric's letter into a pouch at her belt, not into the Book of Shadows — paper and wards don't mix, and this letter is owed to Thorn, not to the Lantern.

"We'll see this into her hands, and your words with it." She meets Osric's eyes. "If we find Hob Carrow, we'll tell him what you said about the sharing."

Then she turns to Pell and Bram, settling her pack and moving toward the door.

"Case to Thorn before we do anything else. After that, if the road's been kind, the Red Sheaf for Hob — but not at the cost of the sunset."

scenes.narration:
Osric hears the three of them out at the door. He takes Pell's offer with a short nod and no more. To Sefa he says only "Hob'll do it straight," and to Bram's *mind yourself* he says "Always do." Then he takes up his place in the doorway again, arms folded, and watches them go.

Outside, the glare is hard after the cool of the house. Bram wraps the case in his bedroll, checks that the flap of his pack covers it, glances once at the sun and sets off down the track at a road pace he could hold all day. Sefa follows a few steps behind him with the letter in the pouch at her belt. Pell lets them get ahead, thirty paces or so, and walks the track with his eyes on the ground.

This is his trade, and the dust makes it easy. Below the yard the track runs along the lip of the lower cut, a wide shelf of packed white spoil with the drop of the cutting on the left. The quarrymen's prints from yesterday go down it, soft-edged and blurred by the night. On top of them are three fresh sets, which are their own from this morning, coming up. Nothing else. Nobody has come up or gone down since dawn, on foot or on hooves.

He's crouched over a crisp heel-print that he's fairly sure is Bram's when the ground under his boots makes a sound like a cracked plate.

Then it's gone.

The crust of spoil drops out from under Pell in a single slab, and old timber goes with it. It was a gallery roof, its beams rotted to sponge under a skin of white dust a foot thick. Pell falls eight feet in a roar of chalk and splinters and lands in water. The cold shuts his breath off. His shoulder hits stone under the surface hard enough to jar his teeth, and something heavy comes down after him: a squared block, shaken loose from the edge of the hole, which slides off the rubble and settles across his left shin. It pins the leg to the gallery floor and doesn't move.

It's a bruising fall, a cracked-rib kind of ache down one side and a scraped forearm. Nothing is broken that he can feel. He's lightly hurt, and soaked to the chest.

The water is chest-deep, black and cold enough to make his fingers stupid. Daylight comes down through the ragged hole above him in a white shaft full of falling dust. By that light he can see a low gallery running off into the dark in both directions. The walls glitter faintly along one side where something rose-white has grown across the stone like frost. Water trickles somewhere he can't see, a thin steady seep. When he looks at the stone by his chest, the waterline sits a little higher on it than it did when he landed. It's slow. Hours slow, not minutes.

Then the block on his leg. It's dressed stone, a mason's work and not rubble, about as long as a man is tall and squared on every face. He shoves at it with both hands and it doesn't shift a hair, and from down here, with his leg under it, he has nothing to push against. Just under the waterline on the face turned toward him, his fingers find cut lines in the stone. Deliberate curves, a ring of them, and short straight marks around the ring like tallies. In this light he can't make out the shape. Across the gallery lies one of the roof beams that came down with him. It's half sound, old oak, long enough to work as a lever from the lip of the hole.

He can see it plainly enough: a rope round the block, the beam under its edge, two people above pulling and prying, and it would roll off his leg in a few minutes. Alone, with no purchase, it's a long hard fight.

---

Up on the track, Bram and Sefa hear the crack, then the crash and the slap of water, and they turn to see a plume of white dust standing where Pell was. Thirty paces back along the lip of the cut there's a hole in the track the size of a cart bed, and no Pell.

In the doorway of the warden's house, Osric Hale's arms come unfolded.

"That's over the old third gallery," he calls down the yard, already walking, not running. "Don't stand at the edge. It goes in a ring."

---

*(Out of game: Pell took 7 bludgeoning from the fall and is at 26 of 33. He can try to free his leg alone once an hour with a Strength (Athletics) check against DC 18, and each failed try costs him a few hit points. The water is rising slowly. Bram and Sefa together, with a rope and the beam, can shift the block in a few minutes with no roll and no cost.)*

Bram, Sefa, you're thirty paces off, the hole is in front of you and Osric is coming down the yard behind you. What do you do?

- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell! Can you hear me?”

I stop well short of the broken ground and set my pack down away from the collapse. Pulling out my rope, I tie a loop in one end big enough for Pell to put over his shoulders.

“Hale! Where’s solid ground—and is there another way into that gallery?”

I look for a sound tree, post or exposed rock to anchor the rope, keeping away from the crumbling lip. “Sefa, keep clear of the edge. Let’s not put three of us down there.”

If Pell answers, I call toward his voice: “Rope coming. Are you in water? Can you hold on?” I’ll toss him the loop from firm ground if he’s within reach, rather than step onto the unsupported rim.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa runs the few paces toward the hole but stops well back from the edge, as Osric said. Her heart is beating high in her throat.

"Pell!" she calls down, steadying her voice. "Pell, answer if you can! Keep still if you've a leg under you; don't dig about."

She drops to one knee a safe distance back, one hand on the ground, and glances quickly toward the lip of the cut and the warden.

"Is there a way down, Osric? A gallery, a ladder?" She raises her voice so Bram can hear. "Bram, we need rope if you have it. We don't haul the world up ourselves — we make a line to him first, light and then hand."

scenes.narration:
Bram's voice goes down the hole: "Pell! Can you hear me?" Sefa's follows a breath later, high and steady: "Pell, answer if you can!" Dust still hangs over the hole in a slow white cloud and drifts off down the cut. Whatever answer comes up from below belongs to Pell.

Osric reaches them on the inner side of the track, against the cut face. He doesn't go any nearer the hole than they have. He stamps once with his heel, and the ground under his boot gives back a dull, solid knock, not the hollow sound the spoil made.

"Here. This side." He scuffs the white skin of dust aside with his boot, and grey rock shows underneath, smooth and old. "Living stone, from the face out about two strides. Past that it's spoil over timber, all the way round the hole. That's the ring." He nods toward the lip without stepping toward it. "Edge'll take a man lying flat. Not standing."

Bram has already put his pack down well back on the rock, with the bedroll and the case inside it. He shakes out the hempen rope and ties a bowline in one end, loose enough to go over a man's shoulders. When he looks for an anchor, Osric doesn't wait to be asked. There's an iron ring set into the face about fifteen feet uphill of the hole, rusty but leaded deep into the rock. It was a guy-point for the lifting frame, back when the frame stood here. Bram hauls on it with his weight and it doesn't give. He runs the rope through it and takes a turn round his own waist. Now the line can go over the lip without anyone standing on it.

"Other way in?" Osric looks down the cut toward the foot of the lower face. "Old adit, down the bottom. Boarded. Water's to the lintel since before my time." He shakes his head once. "That hole's your way in."

Sefa kneels on the grey rock with one hand flat on the stone. Osric looks at her when she talks about the line, the light and then the hand, and he seems to agree with the order of it.

"There's a pinch-bar in the near shed. Iron. Longer than me." He's already turning toward it. "Get him out quick. Cold sits in you down there."

He goes off across the yard at his walking pace, the same as before, but he doesn't fold his arms.

Bram stands at the anchor with the loop ready in his hand. The lip of the hole is about ten feet off across the bad ground, and he can lie flat on it or throw from where he is. Sefa kneels two strides back on the living rock. Osric is at the near shed, dragging the door open.

*(Out of game: Pell's answer, if he gives one, comes from his own scene. Bram's throw goes as soon as there's a voice to throw toward.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*The cold punches the breath out of him and for a second there's nothing but black water and the roar of chalk settling. Then the roof-runner in him takes over: don't thrash, don't waste it.*

*He gets his head clear, spits dust, and puts two fingers in his mouth. Two whistles — sharp, long, the loudest he's got — up the shaft of light. Then his voice after them:*

"BRAM! SEFA! Track's given way — I'm down a hole, thirty paces back of you, lip of the cut! Leg's pinned, I'm not dying — DON'T come running or you'll be down here with me! Walk the edge, test it, follow my shouts!"

*He keeps calling every few breaths so they can home on him, and while he waits he works. One hand goes over his shoulder to the pack, fumbling the silk rope free with fingers that don't want to close; he gets a loop of it round the block end-to-end, as low under the water as he can reach, and knots it off so there's a line to pass up when they arrive. He eyes the fallen beam across the gallery — out of reach from here, but Bram can drop in for it, or they can fish it with the rope.*

*Between shouts, almost against his will, his fingertips go back to the cut lines on the block face. He traces them slowly: the ring, the tallies around it, whatever's in the middle. Mason's work, dressed stone, carved — in a quarry that cuts chalk for building. Someone put this stone here, under the track, once. And Hale stood very still about it.*

*Louder, up the hole, when he hears boots:* "Rope's already round the block — I'll throw you the end! There's a beam down here long enough to lever it. One of you on the rope, one on the beam, and mind the edge — this whole shelf's rotten!"

scenes.narration:
The whistles go up the shaft of light hard enough to hurt in that low stone room. Two of them, long and sharp, and the gallery throws them back at him from both directions. His voice follows them up the hole: *Bram, Sefa, the track's gone, leg's pinned, I'm not dying, don't come running.*

Answers come down almost on top of it. First his own name in Bram's voice, then Sefa's, higher and steadier, telling him to keep still. Further off is Osric's gravel, raised for once: something about the old third gallery, and *don't stand at the edge, it goes in a ring.* Then boots on stone, heavy and careful, not running. Pell keeps calling every few breaths so they have something to steer by. Each shout costs him more of the warmth in his chest.

He works between the shouts. Getting the silk rope out of the pack takes longer than it should, because the cold has already reached his fingers and they close like a fist in a mitten. The block lies wedged on rubble, and at its far end a broken slab of roof props it a hand's width off the floor. That's enough of a gap. He feeds the rope through under the water by feel, brings it back over the top and ties it off. It takes him three tries, and the knot he ends up with is one he'd be ashamed of on a roof. It holds when he hauls on it. He coils the free end over his arm, ready to throw.

Then his fingertips go back to the cut lines, slowly this time.

The ring is a true circle, about two hands across, cut clean and deep. Inside it, in the middle, is a smaller raised disc, smooth as a coin. Straight grooves run out from that disc to the ring, more than a dozen of them, evenly spaced like spokes on a wheel, or rays. Around the outside of the ring the short tallies stand in groups: three, then one, then four, then a long stroke laid crossways, then more of them. There are too many groups to count with numb fingers, and they carry on around the curve and down below where his hand can reach. These aren't scratches. A mason cut them with a chisel and meant them to last. Then he laid the stone face-down in a flooded gallery under a road.

On the side of the block away from him, where the dressed face meets the gallery wall, the stone isn't stone. When his knuckles brush it, it's softer and chalkier, like old plaster.

A hempen loop drops down the shaft of light and slaps the water a yard from his chest, with Bram's voice behind it. Above, past the ragged rim of the hole, he can see a slice of white sky and dust still drifting across it. Across the gallery the oak beam lies half in the water where it fell, too far away for him to reach.

The waterline on the stone by his ribs hasn't moved that he can see. The cold has, though. It has reached his knees and hips and settled into the leg under the block, which he can no longer feel properly.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa watches Bram set the rope and anchor it, then pushes herself flat onto the rock.

"I'll bring light to the lip, not my weight. Give me room."

She picks up a fist-sized piece of white stone, touches it, and the Lantern's light wakes in it — clear and steady, bright as a lantern. She crawls forward on her belly, keeping to the ground Osric stamped solid, and stops just short of the broken edge. One arm stretched out, she holds the lit stone over the hole so its light drops down without her wrist bearing anything.

"Can you see him, Pell?" she calls. "Take the rope first if it reaches you. Don't try to climb until you've told us how you're lying." Her voice is steadier than her pulse. "And answer twice for yes if you can't speak well."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I throw the loop into the hole from the solid rock, paying out rope so it can reach below rather than hang tight across the opening.

“Pell! There’s a loop coming down. Get it under your arms if you can, and tell us when you’re secure. We won’t haul until you’re ready.”

I brace at the anchor, keeping the line controlled without pulling it up. “Sefa, can you get light down there? I still can’t see him.”

I listen for Pell’s voice or a splash and watch the rope for movement.

scenes.narration:
Sefa goes down flat on the grey rock and works forward on her elbows. Two strides out, the living stone ends under her and the white crust begins. She feels the difference through her stays: rock, then something that gives a hair, like a mattress over boards. It creaks once, a dry creak deep down in the timber. It holds. Osric said it would hold a body lying flat, and it does. She stops an arm's length short of the ragged rim, puts her fingers on the lump of chalk in her hand, and the Lantern's light wakes in it. It's clear and white, as bright as a hooded lantern with the shutter open. She holds it out over the drop at arm's length.

The light falls down the hole and the dark below opens up.

The gallery is lower than she'd pictured, the old roof barely a man's height above the water. The water is black and very still except round Pell. He's there, in it to the chest, soaked white with chalk on his hair and shoulders, his face pale against the dark. A coil of pale silk rope hangs over one of his arms. Bram's hempen loop floats a yard from him where it landed. Past him, a squared block of dressed stone lies under the surface. Its near edge shows as a straight pale line in the water. The rest of it is a shape, and the shape runs across where his left leg ought to be. Across the gallery an oak beam lies half-sunk, one end propped on the rubble. Along one wall something rose-white catches her light and glitters like frost on a pane.

At the far end of the block, where it meets the gallery wall, there's a seam of old grey plaster. As her light passes over it, the plaster seems to hold the light a breath longer than wet stone should. Then it's just plaster again. It could be the water throwing her light back. She's flat on her belly at the edge of a hole, and her arm is starting to shake.

Bram, back at the guy-ring, feeds out slack until the hempen line lies loose over the lip instead of drawn tight across it. He keeps the turn round his waist and doesn't pull. Now that there's light he can see down along the rope, and he can see what Pell shouted up a minute ago: *leg pinned, rope's round the block, there's a beam down here, one on the rope, one on the beam.* All of it is as the man said. The loop is there for Pell when he wants it. Nobody is going to haul a man whose leg is under a stone.

Boots come across the yard behind them, steady, and something iron scrapes on stone. Osric comes back along the cut face with the pinch-bar on his shoulder. It's black iron, longer than he is, and one end is flattened into a chisel lip. He stops on the living rock next to Bram, looks down the line, then at Sefa lying on the crust with her light held out.

"Don't haul him," he says. "Leg's under it. Pull now and you leave the leg." He shrugs the bar down off his shoulder and stands it on its foot. "Block first. Bar goes in under the near edge from the lip, lying down. His rope off the block comes up to whoever's on the ring. Bar lifts, rope rolls it. Two of you, few minutes." He looks at the light and the hole, and his voice drops. "He's been in that cold long enough."

He holds the bar out across the gap toward Bram, handle first. He doesn't step onto the crust to do it.

"You've the weight for the bar. I'll take the ring." Then, to Sefa, without turning his head: "Keep that light where it is. Can you hold it and him both talking?"

 (Out of game: none of these four needed a roll. Each was routine and safe, so each simply happens, as the turn showed or as below.)

1) Sefa's light: Light is a cantrip and always works. The chalk lump in her hand lights up, and she holds it over the hole lying flat. The crust under her creaks but holds.
2) Sefa's call: the turn left this out, and I'm sorry for that. Her voice goes down the shaft clearly: "Can you see him, Pell? Take the rope first if it reaches you. Don't try to climb until you've told us how you're lying. And answer twice for yes if you can't speak well." Pell's answer comes from his own scene.
3) Bram's loop: it was already down from last round and lies floating a yard from Pell. Bram pays out more slack, so the line lies loose over the lip and isn't pulled tight across it.
4) Bram's brace: he keeps the turn round his waist and holds the line through the guy-ring without pulling. It stays where he wants it.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*The hemp slaps the water and Pell nearly laughs — teeth chattering too hard for it to come out right.*

"Got your rope! Don't haul yet!" *He ties Bram's loop to the free end of his own silk line with a knot his fingers can still manage, then shouts up:* "Mine's round the block, yours is tied to mine — take up the slack, slow, and tell me when it's taut. Don't heave till I say, or you'll roll it the wrong way and take the leg with it!"

*He gets his weight as far back as the pinned shin allows, both hands flat on the block's upper edge.*

"Sefa — the beam's down here, old oak, two yards off me in the water. I can't reach it. Either Bram drops a second line and I'll try to snag it, or one of you comes down the *far* side of the hole, where the rubble's piled — it'll take weight better than the lip. Osric! You said the third gallery runs in a ring — is there a way in that isn't a hole in the road? Doesn't matter. Just tell them where the ground's sound!"

*Low, to himself, forehead against the cold stone a moment:* "Sun on a wheel. Tallies round it. Face down under a road." *He breathes.* "Later, Pell."

*Then up again, voice steady by force:* "Right. Bram — slack up. When it's taut, pull north, toward the house — the block's propped on a slab that side, that's the way it wants to go. Pull on three. Sefa, if that beam gets to me I'll set it; if it doesn't, don't wait on it, I've one good leg and a bad temper and that's enough for a stone."

"One — two —"

scenes.narration:
Bram's hempen loop is in Pell's fist and his silk line is over his arm. His fingers have gone thick and slow, but he joins the two the only way they'll still manage: a sheet bend, pulled tight with his teeth. It isn't pretty and it holds. Now the line runs from the far end of the block, through his ugly knot, through this one, up out of the water and over the lip into the white sky. When he lets go, the rope sags back toward the hole and lies there slack, waiting for whoever is on the other end.

His shout goes up after it: *don't haul yet, take up the slack, tell me when it's taut.*

Light comes down while he's still shouting. It's white and steady, not daylight. It drops down the hole from a point just over the rim, and the gallery jumps into view around him. The low roof is barely a man's height over the water. The rose-white crust along the wall glitters like hoarfrost. The oak beam lies two yards off, one end propped on the rubble, close enough to look at and too far to reach. Sefa's voice comes down with the light. She's close, and lying flat by the sound of it. *Can you see him, Pell? Take the rope first if it reaches you. Don't try to climb until you've told us how you're lying. Answer twice for yes if you can't speak well.*

He's already told her how he's lying. He keeps going: the beam, the far side, a second line.

Osric answers him. Pell can't see him. His gravel voice comes from somewhere back from the edge, on the side toward the cut face.

"Far side's no better. Spoil over timber, all round the hole. Only sound rock is this side, two strides off the face." There's a pause, and something iron scrapes on stone up there. "No other way in. Adit's under water."

Then, louder, aimed down the hole at Pell:

"Rope runs through the ring in the face. That's uphill, toward the face, not toward the house. It pulls the way the ring lies." Another pause. "There's a pinch-bar up here. Bar under the near edge lifts it off the slab. Then the rope rolls it. Pull without the bar and you drag stone along your shin."

He stops there. He's said his piece.

Pell puts his forehead to the stone for a moment. The light from above reaches a little way through the black water, enough to make out what his fingers already know: a pale ring, the disc in its middle, the straight rays between, and the tallies running round the outside and down into the dark where the light gives out. *Sun on a wheel.* The cold seeps up from the leg he can't feel properly and into his hips.

He gets his weight back as far as the pinned shin allows and puts both hands flat on the block's upper edge.

"One — two —"

Above him the rope still lies slack over the lip. The block doesn't move, and the water by his ribs sits where it sat.

*(Out of game: whether the line comes taut, and whether anyone pulls or brings the bar in on three, is for Bram and Sefa in their own scene.)*

 (Out of game: none of the four needed a roll, and all four happen in the turn as written. Pell ties the sheet bend and it holds, his calls up the hole carry, he tells Sefa about the beam and the far side, and Osric says there's no other way in.)

Sefa asked whether you could see Bram, and told you to take the rope first if it reaches you. She said not to try climbing until you had said how you are lying. If you cannot speak well, she wants you to answer twice for yes. You have already told her how you lie, so you press on with the beam, the far side and a second line.

Osric answered your questions in his gravel voice. The far side is no better, he said: spoil over timber all round the hole. The only sound rock is on this side, two strides off the face. There is no other way in, because the adit is under water. Then he called down to you directly. The rope runs through the ring in the face, which is uphill, toward the face and not toward the house. It pulls the way the ring lies. He has a pinch-bar up there. With the bar under the near edge he can lift the block off the slab, and then the rope will roll it. Without the bar, he said, a pull would drag stone along your shin. Then he said no more.

Your sheet bend, pulled tight with your teeth, is ugly and it holds. The line now runs from the far end of the block, through your knot and Bram's, up out of the water and over the lip into the white sky. When you let go, it sagged back toward the hole and lay slack.

A steady white light comes down the hole from a point just over the rim. It is not daylight. The gallery jumps into view. The low roof is barely a man's height above the water. The rose-white crust along the wall glitters like hoarfrost. The oak beam lies two yards off, one end propped on the rubble, close enough to look at and too far to reach.

You put your forehead to the stone for a moment. The light reaches a little way into the black water, enough to show what your fingers already knew: a pale ring, the disc in its middle, the straight rays between, and the tallies running round the outside and down into the dark. The cold seeps up from the leg you can't feel properly and into your hips.

You get your weight back as far as the pinned shin allows and put both hands flat on the block's upper edge. You begin the count aloud: one, two.

Above you the rope still lies slack over the lip. The block doesn't move, and the water by your ribs sits where it sat.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Aye. Take the line.”

I hand control of the rope over to Osric before unwinding it from my waist, then take the pinch-bar. Keeping my weight spread flat, I ease forward on my belly with the bar alongside me, following his directions.

“Pell, we’re lifting the block, not you. Tell us if it shifts against your leg. Once there’s room, pull clear if you can.”

By Sefa’s light, I work the flattened end beneath the block’s near edge as Osric indicated, looking for a sound purchase.

“Ready, Hale? Slow, together.”

Once he has the block’s rope ready, I bear down steadily on the bar, aiming to lift it just enough for Osric to roll it clear of Pell’s leg.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa braces her elbows on the white crust, grips the lit stone in both hands, and lets her breath out slow so the light stops shaking.

"I'll hold it, Osric. Do what needs doing."

She keeps her eyes down the shaft and calls, calm and clear:

"Pell, don't pull and don't dig. The block is on your leg, not through you. We lift it, then we take you up. While they set the bar, get Bram's loop under your arms if it's near you — but don't fight it. Keep your head up, and tell me twice if you can hear me and you're still with us."

scenes.narration:
Bram unwinds the hemp from his waist and puts it into Osric's fists at the ring. The warden takes two turns of it round his own forearm and plants his boots on the grey rock. "Got it." Bram takes the bar.

It's heavy, cold black iron that's warm only where Osric's hands were. Bram goes down flat with it lying alongside him and works forward on his belly and elbows the way Sefa did. Under his mail the crust takes his weight differently than it took hers. It gives a long dry groan deep in the timber, and white dust sifts off the rim of the hole into the light. It holds. Two lengths of a man from the rock, he can see straight down past Sefa's outstretched arms.

Sefa has her elbows dug into the crust and the lit chalk gripped in both hands. She breathes out slowly and the light stops shaking. It drops down the shaft clear and steady and lies on the black water. Her voice follows it: *don't pull, don't dig, the block's on your leg and not through you, get Bram's loop under your arms if it's near you, tell me twice if you can hear me.* Then Bram's, lower: *we're lifting the block, not you. Tell us if it shifts against your leg.*

By her light Bram finds the near edge of the block, a straight pale line under the water, and feeds the chisel lip of the bar down along it. The first time it skates off dressed stone. The second time it finds the gap where the block's edge sits on rubble, and it bites. He feels it bite all the way up the iron.

"Ready, Hale? Slow, together."

"Slow," Osric says from the ring.

Bram bears down. For a long moment nothing gives except his shoulders. Then the block lifts off the rubble a finger's width, then a hand's, and the bar bows a little under him. Behind him the hemp creaks through the old iron ring as Osric leans back on it, steady and not jerking. The line comes taut over the lip and the knots take the strain. The block turns, slowly, a big squared shape rolling over on its long side through the water toward the face, the way the ring pulls. Black water heaves up round it and slaps the gallery walls. Then there's a sound under the surface, stone settling onto stone, and the bar goes light in Bram's hands.

The block is off the leg. It lies a stride away against the rubble, turned a quarter over, and the face that was hidden now faces up.

It's just under the water now, and Sefa's light falls straight on it.

She sees a true circle cut deep and clean, a smooth raised disc in the middle, and straight rays running out from the disc to the ring, more than a dozen of them, evenly spaced. Sefa knows that shape. Every hospice chapel in the Lower City that took Lathander's coin had one over the door. It's the Morninglord's sun as the old temples cut it, a sunburst on a wheel. Short mason's marks run round the outside of the ring in groups. They catch her eye the way a line of handwriting does across a room, as if they're meant to be read. From up here and through moving water she can't make them out.

At the far end of the block, where it had pressed against the gallery wall, the old grey plaster has cracked as the stone rolled. A dark seam has opened there, no wider than a finger. Something behind it, deep in the gap, answers her light with a faint milky glow, like moonlight through a dirty pane. It doesn't fade the way the reflection on the water does. For a breath the lump of chalk in her hands is warmer than her own skin.

Up at the ring, Osric has seen the stone's face too. He stands very still with the hemp still wound round his forearm, and doesn't say anything about it.

"Get him up," he says. "Loop's there."

*(Out of game: no roll; two of you on a lever and a rope shift the block with no cost, as I flagged. Pell's leg is free. How he comes up, and whether he answers Sefa, comes from his own scene.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell bites off the "three" before it leaves his teeth.*

"HOLD! Hold — nobody pull!"

*He lets his breath out against the stone. Hale was right and he was wrong, and down here that's the kind of wrong that costs a shin.*

"Hale — heard you. You're right, I had it backwards; the ring's uphill, so it rolls toward the face. Your bar first, then the rope, in that order. I'm not going anywhere." *A cracked laugh.* "Clearly."

"Here's how I want it, then, and tell me if the ground says otherwise. Hale, you're the one who knows where it's sound — you work the bar. Two strides off the face, like you said. Get it under the near edge and lift; the second this thing comes off the slab I'll feel it and I'll shout. Bram, you're on the rope — take the slack up now, slow, till it's taut, and *hold* it there. Don't pull till I say. The moment Hale's got it lifted, you haul toward the face, steady, no jerking. Sefa, keep that light on me — it's the best thing anyone's done all morning — and keep talking to me. scenes.narration:
Pell bites the "three" off before it leaves his teeth. *Hold, nobody pull.* The shout goes up the shaft and the gallery throws it back at him. Then he gives them the rest of it, and every word costs him breath: the ring's uphill, the bar goes in first and the rope comes after, and if he stops answering they should drag him out and worry about the leg later.

Up above, they had already set it up the other way round.

The first voice to come down is Bram's, low and close, from just over the rim: *we're lifting the block, not you. Tell us if it shifts against your leg.* Osric's voice comes from further back, from the ring. Iron scrapes on dressed stone somewhere near Pell's knee and skates off. Then it scrapes again, lower, and stops with a short grinding bite that Pell feels through the water and up the bones of his pinned leg. He keeps his hands flat on the block's edge and his weight back, and he waits.

"Ready, Hale? Slow, together."

"Slow."

For a long moment nothing changes except the sound of a big man breathing hard through his nose above him. Then the pressure on Pell's shin eases. It comes off slowly, the width of a finger and then the width of a hand, the block rising off the rubble the way a door comes off its hinges. Somewhere up in the white the hemp creaks through the old iron ring. The line over his arm draws taut, his ugly knot takes the strain and holds, and the block rolls. It goes slowly and heavily, turning on its long side away from him toward the face, the way Osric said it would. Black water heaves up round his chest and slaps the walls. Something settles under the surface with a deep stone-on-stone knock.

His leg is free.

At first it doesn't feel like anything, just a weight on the end of his hip that won't answer. Then the blood finds its way back in, and pins and needles run from his knee to his toes, so sharp that he has to set his teeth. He can move his foot when he tells it to, and it hurts. A bruise is coming up along the shin where the stone sat. It isn't broken. He's sure of that the moment the ankle turns properly under him.

The block lies a stride away now, a quarter-turn over against the rubble, and the face he was tracing blind is turned up under Sefa's light. He doesn't need his fingers for it any more. The ring is there, with the smooth disc and the rays running out to the edge, and the tallies run round the outside in their groups, all the way round now, none of them hidden below. At the block's far end, where it had pressed against the gallery wall, the old grey plaster has cracked as the stone rolled. A dark seam a finger wide has opened there. Something deep inside it is pale. From where Pell stands, chest-deep and shaking, it could be wet chalk catching the light from above. It could also be something else.

His last words went up the shaft along with all the rest: *you and I are going to have a word about what a mason's sun-wheel is doing face-down under your road.* No answer comes down from the ring. There's no grunt and no "later", only the creak of the hemp settling as Osric takes the strain off it. Then the gravel comes, flat:

"Get him up. Loop's there."

Bram's hempen loop floats at Pell's chest, still joined to the silk line by the sheet bend he tied with his teeth. Above him the rim of the hole is ragged and white against the sky. The cold sits in him from the hips down, and it isn't going anywhere while he stays in this water.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds the light steady over the water, though her arms are shaking again from something other than the cold.

"Pell! The loop — it's in the water about a yard to your left. Get it under your arms, not round the leg. Tell us when it's on you, and then leave the climbing to them."

She doesn't take her eyes from the dark below, but she marks the place in her mind exactly as he'd seen it from above — the block's face, the sunburst, the bright seam in the wall — and lets the thought settle like a stone in her chest. This is a matter for when the man is warm and on the road.

"Osric," she says, quieter, without turning her head, "that stone we carved. You know it?"

She listens for the answer, but her attention stays on the shaft.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, block’s clear. Can you get the loop under your arms?”

I ease the pinch-bar back from the hole and lay it flat beside me, careful not to knock the loose rim.

“Hale, make sure we’re hauling Pell’s line, not the block’s. Slow once he says he’s secure.”

I stay spread flat, ready to guide Pell past the broken lip without dragging his injured leg against it. “Sefa, keep the light on him. We’ll look at the stone once he’s out.”

When Pell confirms he’s secure, I help guide him up as Osric hauls, then work backward toward the living rock rather than stand on the crust.

Sefa's voice goes down the shaft, low and clear: *the loop's a yard to your left, under your arms and not round the leg, tell us when it's on you.* Bram's follows a breath later from a little further along the rim: *block's clear, can you get the loop under your arms?* The light in her hands holds steady over the black water.

Bram pulls the pinch-bar back from the hole a hand's width at a time and lays it flat on the crust beside him. The rim doesn't shed so much as a crumb. Then he looks back at the ring. "Hale, make sure we're hauling Pell's line, not the block's."

Osric already has the hemp in both fists. He looks down the length of it to the lip, then at the hole, and shakes his head once.

"Same line." He lifts the rope a little so Bram can see it run. "Ring, loop, then his knot to the silk, and the silk's round the stone. Haul now and he comes up with a block hung off him." He lets the rope settle again. "He casts the silk off down there. Knot or knife. Then it's his line."

He says it loud enough to carry down the shaft, and leaves it at that.

Then Sefa asks her question, quietly, without turning her head. Osric doesn't answer straight away. His eyes go to the rim of the hole and the white light coming up out of it, and stay there.

"Never seen it." It comes out flat. "Thirty years on this hill. Didn't know there was a face on anything down there." He shifts his grip on the hemp. "Sun's the Morninglord's. Any fool knows that much." He thinks a moment. "In Beregost they say the temple's first stones came off this hill. Before the town was a town. That's the old men talking." He tips his head toward the shaft. "Him first."

He doesn't say anything more about the stone. He hasn't looked at the sunburst again since it came up.

Down below, under Sefa's light, the block lies a quarter-turn over in the water with its face to the roof. The finger-wide seam at its far end is still dark. Deep in it the pale something still gives back her light, dimly, and doesn't fade.

The hemp lies slack over the lip, running down to the loop at Pell's chest and the ugly knot below it. Osric keeps his boots planted at the ring with his hands on the rope and doesn't take it up. Bram lies flat at the rim, ready to guide. Nobody pulls until the word comes up from below.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell gets the loop over his head and under his arms and cinches it. Then he doesn't shout "pull."*

"One breath, Bram. Hold the line — don't haul yet."

*One stride, on the leg that doesn't feel like his, hand on the wall to keep from going under. He puts his face close to the block's far end where the plaster cracked, and lifts his chin at the light.*

"Sefa — bring it a hand to your left. On the seam, where the plaster's split."

*He gets a dagger out — not to pry, just to have a blade to probe with instead of fingers he can't trust — and slides the point into the dark seam, slow, to feel whether the pale thing inside is chalk, bone, cloth or metal. Ten heartbeats, no more. He's counting them. If it's loose and comes to the blade, it comes up with him in his shirt; if it's set in the wall, it stays, and he marks exactly where the seam sits against the wheel so he'll know the spot again.*

*Then he turns, wades back to the shaft, gets both hands on the hemp and sets his good foot against the rubble.*

"Right. Now haul. Steady — I'll walk the wall." *Up the shaft, lighter, through chattering teeth:* "And somebody get a fire in that kettle, Hale, because I'm about to drip on your floor."

scenes.narration:
Pell gets the hemp loop over his head and works it down under his arms. His fingers fumble the bowline twice before it cinches against his ribs. His voice goes up the shaft: *one breath, Bram, hold the line, don't haul yet.* Then *Sefa, a hand to your left, on the seam.*

He takes one stride on a leg that feels like it belongs to someone else. The rubble shifts under his boot, the black water climbs to his collarbone, and his palm on the gallery wall is the only thing keeping him upright. The block lies a quarter-turn over beside him with its face to the roof. He puts his face close to its far end, where the old grey plaster has cracked away from the gallery wall.

The light from above stays where it was, white and steady on the sunburst, and the seam sits at the edge of it. Up close it's a dark crack a finger wide, running from just above the waterline down into the water. Deep inside, the pale thing is still there. From here it doesn't look like wet chalk. Chalk would be catching the light from the shaft. This is a dim, milky glow that seems to come from inside it, the way a horn lantern looks from the street with the shutter half down. It doesn't flicker with the water.

He draws a dagger and slides the point into the crack, slowly, counting.

At three the blade goes through crumbling plaster as if it were stale bread. At five it touches something. It isn't stone: there's no grit and no drag. The point makes a small, clean *tick* and skates off a smooth surface that curves away under it. He tries again, a little lower, and gets the same tick on the same curve. He knows the sound from window glass, though this is thicker and duller. At eight he presses gently to see if it will rock. It doesn't. It sits in something, a niche behind the plaster, and whatever it is is wider than the crack by a good deal. Nothing that size is coming out through a finger-wide gap unless someone breaks the plaster. At ten he draws the blade out, and a curl of old grey plaster comes with it and falls into the water.

It's set, so it stays.

He marks the place against the wheel. The seam lies off the end of the block, in line with the point of the ring where the long crossways stroke sits among the tallies. It's about a forearm above the waterline as the block lies now. He'd find it again in the dark.

Then he turns and wades back to the shaft. Every step sends pins and needles up the bruised shin. He gets both hands on the hemp above the loop and sets his good foot against the rubble. *Now haul, steady, I'll walk the wall.* After that, through his teeth, the bit about a fire in the kettle.

The rope doesn't come taut. It hangs slack from the rim. The gravel voice comes down the shaft from somewhere back toward the face, flat and loud enough to carry:

"Silk's still on the stone. Your knot. Cast it off, or I'm hauling the block up with you."

The hemp in Pell's fists runs down past his chest to the loop. Below the loop sits the ugly sheet bend he tied with his teeth, and from there the pale silk runs off through the water to the block.

*(Out of game: the sheet bend joining the loop to the silk round the block is still tied, and nobody up top will haul until it's off. Cast it off, by knot or knife, if you want to go up.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, the silk below your loop is still tied to the block. Undo it or cut it clear—whichever you can manage. Tell us when it’s free and the loop’s secure.”

I stay flat, keeping my hands ready at the lip.

“No hurry on the knot, Hale. We wait for his word.”

I watch Pell by Sefa’s light, ready to help guide him over the edge once the line is clear and Osric starts hauling.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't turn from the shaft. Her arms tremble, and she locks them, letting the weight settle through her shoulders into the rock.

"The Morninglord's, then. That would explain it, but it can wait." Her voice is low, only for the warden. "Pell first. And until he's warm, that stone is just a stone."

She calls down again, clear as a bell:

"We're not hauling until you tell us. Cast off the silk — cut it or work the knot. Keep the hempen loop. When it's on you, say 'ready' so we can hear it, and we'll bring you up slow."

Bram's voice goes down the shaft, low and even: *the silk below your loop's still tied to the block, undo it or cut it, tell us when it's free.* Then he settles flat on the crust again with his hands at the lip. Beside him the pinch-bar lies along the rim where he left it. The crust under his mail gives one more long, dry creak and then goes quiet.

"No hurry on the knot, Hale. We wait for his word."

"Aye." Osric doesn't take up an inch of hemp. He stands on the grey rock at the ring with both fists on the rope and his boots planted, the turns still round his forearm.

Sefa's arms have started to shake again. She locks her elbows into the crust and lets the weight sink down through her shoulders, and the light steadies. It falls white and straight down the hole onto the black water and the pale shape of the block under it. Her own voice comes after it, clear: *we're not hauling until you tell us. Cast off the silk, keep the hempen loop, say "ready" when it's on you.*

Then she says the other part quietly, for the warden only, without turning her head. *The Morninglord's, then. That would explain it, but it can wait. Pell first. Until he's warm, that stone is just a stone.*

Osric is quiet long enough that she can hear water trickling somewhere down in the gallery.

"It's a stone till he's out," he says. "After that it's still under my road." He shifts his grip. "Hearth's laid. Kettle's full. I'll light it when he's on the rock, not before. I'm not leaving this rope."

That's all he says, and he looks at nothing but the line.

The hemp lies slack over the lip and runs down past Bram's hands into the shaft of light. Down below, the knot is still between the loop and the silk. The water stirs around the man in it, and the wheel lies face-up under it. At the far end of the block the seam keeps its faint milky glow, steady, just where it was. Nobody up top moves. Whether the word comes, and when, is up to the man in the water.

Sefa's arms have started to shake again. She locks her elbows into the crust and lets the weight sink down through her shoulders, and the light steadies. It falls white and straight down the hole onto the black water and the pale shape of the block under it. Her own voice comes after it, clear: *we're not hauling until you tell us. Cast off the silk, keep the hempen loop, say "ready" when it's on you.*

Then she says the other part quietly, for the warden only, without turning her head. *The Morninglord's, then. That would explain it, but it can wait. Pell first. Until he's warm, that stone is just a stone.*

Osric is quiet long enough that she can hear water trickling somewhere down in the gallery.

"It's a stone till he's out," he says. "After that it's still under my road." He shifts his grip. "Hearth's laid. Kettle's full. I'll light it when he's on the rock, not before. I'm not leaving this rope."

messages.text:
*A bark of a laugh that's half shiver.* "Aye. That'd be the second time today I had it backwards. Hold."

*He doesn't try the block knot — it's under black water and his fingers have stopped being his. The dagger's still in his hand. scenes.narration:
The hemp creaks as Osric shifts his grip at the ring. Pell doesn't try the knot on the block. That knot is under black water, and his fingers have stopped taking orders. The dagger is still in his hand. He pulls the silk tight between the sheet bend and the stone, follows it down into the water with his other hand, and cuts it a forearm short of the block. Wet silk parts easily. The rest of the line goes slack against his chest. He coils it over his shoulder, about forty feet of it, and gets the knife back into its sheath at the second try. A short end of pale silk stays knotted round the block under the water. It looks like a tag on a parcel.

He looks at the block once more. The sunburst faces up into the white light. At the far end the plaster has cracked, and behind it the milky glow shows steady, the same as before.

*Silk's clear. Just me on the line. Haul.*

The rope takes his weight. It doesn't jerk. It comes in slow and even, the pull of a man leaning back on it with his boots planted. Pell walks up the gallery wall with his good foot first and the bruised leg dragging behind. The rubble gives way under him, then the wet stone of the shaft does. Climbing is the one thing his body still does without being told, even numb. Black water pours off him, and then he's out of it. Halfway up the shaft the cold changes. Down in the water it was steady. Up here it's air on wet cloth, and he starts shaking all over, hard enough to rattle his teeth.

He gets his words out anyway, through his teeth, up toward the white: *glass face, a glow of its own, under your road since before you were born. I'll not touch it. I'll not tell Thorn. I'd sooner you told me than I had to guess.*

Up at the ring the hemp keeps coming in, hand over hand. The answer arrives with the rope.

"Didn't know there was a wall down there to be behind." Another pull. "Never been in the third. Nobody has, my time."

His head comes up into daylight. The glare off the white crust is fierce after the gallery. The rim crumbles under his forearms and holds. The hemp drags him over the lip on his belly, the crust groaning dry under him, then across it. Then there's grey rock under his cheek. It's hard and warm from the sun, and it doesn't give at all.

The rope goes slack. Osric's boots stand a stride away. He unwinds the hemp from his forearm, one turn and then the other, and looks down at the man dripping chalk-water onto his living rock.

"Glass I don't know." He coils the end once and drops it. "The low end I know a bit. Men worked long down there, they got heavy in the head. Sleepy. That's the low end." He stops there, as if that was more than he'd meant to say, and his jaw sets. "Fire first. Then the rest, what there is."

He turns and goes off across the yard toward the house, at his walking pace. A moment later his voice comes back over his shoulder, flat:

"Kettle'll be on by the time you can walk."

Behind Pell the hole in the track breathes cold air up into the sun. Somewhere far below, the seep runs on in the dark, and the glow sits in its niche where he left it.

*(Out of game: no roll needed. Cutting a line and climbing out on a held rope are routine for Pell, and Second-Story Work covers the climb. He keeps about forty feet of the silk. The cut end is still tied round the block below.)*

 (Out of game: none of the three needed a roll, and all three happened in the turn. Cutting a line, climbing a held rope and saying something true aren't uncertain for Pell. He cut the silk a forearm short of the block and kept about forty feet of it. He climbed out onto the living rock. Osric heard every word and answered.)

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't speak. She lets the quiet gather, because the next voice out of the hole has to be Pell's.

Her arms are past trembling now; they've gone to that strange steadiness the body finds when it's asked to hold a thing long past its strength. She locks her gaze on the dark water where the light pools, not on the block's face, not on the seam. Just on Pell — the pale shape of him, chest-deep in the cold, the rope floating at his chest.

She is aware, with a kind of distant clarity, of everything around her: Osric's boots on the rock, Bram's spread weight on the crust, the pinch-bar along the rim, and the smell of wet limestone, old and deep. She listens for the sound of a knife on silk, or the drag of wet rope.

A prayer runs through her, not in words — the Lantern knows her anyway. *Keep him steady. Keep the ground under us. Let this not be his death.*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I hold position, making no sudden shift on the creaking crust. My attention stays on Pell and the rope, not the glow below.

“We’re here, Pell.”

I wait for his signal before helping with the haul.
