scenes.narration:
Nobody speaks after Bram's "We're here, Pell." The quiet comes back up the shaft.

Then it breaks from below. There's a short wet rasp, a blade going through silk, and a slap as a slack line hits the water. Pell's voice follows, hoarse with cold and still with that bark of a laugh in it: *silk's clear, just me on the line, haul.*

Behind them Osric leans back on the ring. The hemp comes in hand over hand, slow and even. Under Sefa's light Pell leaves the black water and walks the gallery wall up the shaft, good foot first, the bruised leg dragging after it. Chalk-water pours off him. Halfway up he starts to shake hard. Even so he gets his words out, loud enough to carry past Bram's shoulder: *glass face, a glow of its own, under your road since before you were born. I'll not touch it. I'll not tell Thorn.*

Osric answers between pulls, flat. He didn't know there was a wall down there to be behind. Nobody's been in the third gallery in his time.

Pell's head comes up through the ragged rim right beside Bram. Bram is lying flat with his hands ready. He takes a fistful of wet collar and keeps the man's chest off the broken edge as the hemp drags him over. The rim crumbles under Pell's forearms and holds. Bram works backward on his elbows with him, a hand's width at a time, the crust groaning long and dry under two men's weight, until there's grey rock under both of them. Pell lies on it, dripping. He's pale under the chalk, shaking hard enough to rattle his teeth, and alive.

Sefa's light still hangs over the empty hole. Pell is out of it now, so she can take it back. When she draws her arm in, the white light slides off the water, off the face of the block and the pale tag of silk knotted round it, and up the shaft wall. As it leaves, the seam at the block's far end goes dark with it. The milky glow doesn't linger or fade slowly the way warm embers would. It's there while her light touches it, and then it's gone. The gallery below goes black, and the seep keeps trickling somewhere down in it.

Her prayer gets no answer. All she has is the lump of chalk in her fist, the grey rock under her elbows when she works her way back to it, and the ache that comes into her arms the moment she lets them stop holding.

Osric unwinds the hemp from his forearm, one turn and then the other, and looks down at Pell on his rock. "Glass I don't know," he says. "The low end I know a bit. Men worked long down there, they got heavy in the head. Sleepy." His jaw sets, as if he's said more than he meant to. "Fire first. Then the rest, what there is."

He goes off across the yard toward the house at his walking pace. Over his shoulder: "Kettle'll be on by the time you can walk."

Bram's pack sits where he left it on the living rock, with the case wrapped dry in its bedroll and the flap down. The pinch-bar lies along the rim of the hole on the crust, where Bram laid it. The hemp lies coiled once by the guy-ring. The sun has climbed a little. There's still a long half-day of road ahead and plenty of light to walk it.

A few breaths later, a thin grey thread of smoke goes up from the warden's chimney.

Nothing else here needs anyone this moment. The fire and whatever Osric means by "the rest" are waiting in the house, whenever the three of you want them.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*For a moment Pell just lies there with his cheek on warm rock and lets it not move under him. Then he rolls onto his back, chalk-white from chest to boots, and looks at the sky.*

"Bram. Sefa." *Teeth still going.* "That was clean work. I owe you both a round at the Red Sheaf — I'll stand Hob Carrow one too, since it looks like it's the only coin he'll see this month."

*He gets the hemp loop up over his head with clumsy hands and holds the end out to Bram, then gets his good knee under him and lets whoever's nearest haul him upright. He puts weight on the bruised shin, swears quietly, and finds it holds.*

*Lower, as they help him across the yard toward the smoke:* "Listen. I'm not going to say it in front of him twice, so hear it now. There's a carved stone down there — sun-wheel, tallies round it, mason's work — and behind it, plastered into the wall, something with a glass face that glows on its own. Hale says men who worked the low end got heavy in the head. That's not chalk-dust." *He glances at the pack under Bram's arm.* "The salt grows on the same walls. I don't know what that means yet, and I'm not opening Thorn's case to find out. But I'd like to know what she's really buying before we hand it over for ninety gold."

*At the threshold, dripping on Hale's floor exactly as promised, he goes straight to the hearth and crouches over the kettle like a man hugging a dog.*

"Hale. You said fire first, then the rest. Fire's here." *He looks up, and there's no edge in it — just a soaked man who wants a straight answer from a straight man.* "What did the men say, the ones who got heavy in the head? And how long ago did the last of them say it?"

*To the others, without turning from the heat:* "Quarter of an hour. Then we walk. Sun's not waiting, and neither's that coach — I'll dry on the road."

scenes.narration:
For a while Pell just lies there with his cheek on the warm rock and lets it hold still under him. Then he rolls onto his back, chalk-white from chest to boots, and looks up at the sky. His thanks come out through chattering teeth: clean work, a round owed to each of them at the Red Sheaf, and one for Hob Carrow, since it's the only coin Hob is likely to see this month. He works the hemp loop up over his head with clumsy hands and holds the end out toward Bram.

*(Out of game: whether a hand comes to haul him up, and what Bram and Sefa say to what he tells them, belongs to their own scene.)*

He gets upright and puts weight on the bruised shin. He swears under his breath. It holds. On the way across the yard, low, before the house, he says his piece once for the two of them: the carved sun-wheel with its tallies, the glass face behind the plaster glowing by itself, the men who got heavy in the head, and the salt growing on the same walls. He isn't going to open Thorn's case to find out, but he'd like to know what she's buying before he hands it over for ninety gold.

It's a slow walk on that leg. By the time he reaches the threshold the kettle is starting to tick on its hook.

The long room smells of woodsmoke and damp paper. The fire is small and hot, built the way a man builds one when he doesn't waste fuel. Pell drips on the floor exactly as he promised. Osric looks down at the white puddle spreading from his boots, then at Pell, and says nothing about it. He takes the blanket off the cot, a grey army thing gone thin at the folds, and drops it over Pell's shoulders as Pell crouches at the hearth. Then he hooks the kettle off the fire, pours into a clay mug and sets it on the hearthstone by Pell's knee. It's hot water with something bitter and green in it. It steams.

Pell asks his question, without any edge.

Osric doesn't sit down. He stands by the table where the case used to be and looks at the fire instead of at Pell.

"Heavy in the head. That's how they said it." He gives it one fact at a time. "Sit down on the ledge for a breather, wake up with the lamp guttered. Didn't know they'd gone." A pause. "Worse the longer you stayed down. So I put them on short turns. An hour down, an hour up. Nobody alone."

He's quiet for a moment. The fire cracks.

"Nobody alone, since Tobin."

He goes to the shelf of swollen ledgers and runs a thick finger along the spines without looking, the way a man finds his own door in the dark. He pulls one down, a tally-book with its boards warped, and opens it on the table at a page he doesn't need to search for. Then he turns it round so it faces the hearth and tips his chin at it.

Pell can read it from where he crouches. It's the same big, cramped hand that signed the letter, pressed hard into the paper, under a date three summers gone:

*Tobin Reed, cutter. Found in the low cut end of shift. Drink, in four feet of water.*

"Three years back," Osric says. "Scraping salt, end of the day, on his own. I found him face down." He looks at the line he wrote and not at Pell. "That's what I put."

He leaves the book open and says nothing more. He doesn't say Tobin drank, and he doesn't say he didn't. He stands with his hands at his sides and the fire on one side of his face, and lets the page say what it says.

The water steams in the mug by Pell's knee. Feeling is coming back into his fingers in hot, needling waves. The quarter of an hour he asked for is his, and the sun outside is still well short of noon.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Found yourself a bath, then.” I crouch beside Pell. “Let’s get you warm.”

I take my bedroll from the pack, leaving the sealed case dry inside, and wrap it round his shoulders. “Sefa, how’s his leg? I can carry him if it won’t bear weight.”

I offer Pell my shoulder and help him toward the house, keeping to the living rock and letting him spare the injured leg. I bring my pack; the bar can wait.

“Whatever’s down there will keep. Wet clothes off by the fire first. Then Hale can tell us about those sleepy men.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the light go out of the chalk and tucks the warm stone into her palm like a worry-bead. She doesn't rise all at once; she kneels on the grey rock, takes Pell's wet sleeve, and steadies him.

"Hush now. You're out." Her voice is the one the hospice taught her, soft and unhurried. "Can you walk if Bram and I put a shoulder under you? The kettle's on. There'll be worse things than a chill if you lie here courting it."

She looks over her shoulder toward the warden's door. The smoke goes up straight from the chimney. Then she glances at Bram.

messages.text:
*Pell reads the line twice. He doesn't say anything for a while. He wraps both hands round the clay mug and drinks the bitter green stuff and lets it burn the whole way down.*

"Tobin Reed." *He says it to the fire, not to Hale — the way you say a name so you'll keep it.* "You wrote 'drink' because the alternative was writing something you couldn't put a name to. And a man who can't name what killed his cutter can't very well tell the lads to stop cutting." *He looks up.* "I'm not faulting you. I'd have written the same. I'd have hated it the same, too."

*He pulls the blanket tighter and gets his feet under him, slowly, testing the shin again.*

"Three things, then I'll stop making your floor wet. One — how long has Whitestone been selling that salt? Was it going out before Tobin, or did somebody find a buyer after? Two — did Tull ever send anyone up here who wasn't a carter? A man who asked about the low end, or wanted to see it, or brought his own lamp? Three —" *a nod at the open book* "— does anyone but you and me know that page exists?"

*He lets Hale answer or not. Then he sets the mug down on the hearthstone, empty, and gets his pack back onto his shoulders with hands that mostly work.*

"Here's what I'll do, and you can hold me to it at the Red Sheaf. I'll see the case into Thorn's hands, because that's the job and the lads need the coin. I'll give her your letter and I'll watch her face when she reads *Vandarren*. And I'll ask her — carefully — what an apothecary wants with dye that grows in a drowned gallery where men fall asleep and don't wake." *He pauses at the door.* "I'll not say Tobin's name to anyone. That one's yours."

*Then, to Bram and Sefa, straightening with a grimace:* "Right. I've had my quarter hour and most of Hale's kettle. Bram, the case. Sefa, the letter. I'll walk the back again — and this time I'll walk where the warden says the rock is."

*A last look at Hale from the doorway, dry as the dust:* "Keep off the low end. Nobody alone."

scenes.narration:
Bram crouches beside Pell on the grey rock. "Found yourself a bath, then." He opens his pack and draws out the bedroll the case was wrapped in, taking care that the oak box stays dry in the bottom of the pack. He puts the bedroll round Pell's shoulders. Sefa kneels on his other side. The light has gone out of the chalk, and the stone sits warm in her palm. She takes his wet sleeve. *Hush now. You're out.* It's the hospice voice, soft and unhurried. Then she shakes a blanket out of her own roll, mud on the hems, and wraps it over Bram's bedroll. The cold comes off Pell in waves and she doesn't flinch from it.

Bram gives him a shoulder and they cross the yard on the living rock, Pell sparing the bruised leg. Bram's pack is on his back and the pinch-bar is left where it lies. On the way Bram says the wet clothes should come off by the fire first, and then Hale can tell them about his sleepy men. Sefa says the glass and the sunburst can wait until the case is delivered and they're all sitting at a table. At the threshold Osric looks at the man coming in under two layers of bedding, drops his own grey army blanket on top of them without a word, and goes to the kettle.

That was a quarter of an hour ago. The mug by Pell's knee is empty now.

Pell says Tobin Reed's name to the fire. Then he says the rest to the warden: *you wrote "drink" because the other thing had no name, and you'd not have been able to tell the lads to stop.* Osric listens with his hands at his sides. He doesn't say yes and he doesn't say no. When Pell finishes, the warden reaches over and closes the tally-book. He doesn't slam it. He shuts it the way you'd close a door on a sleeping room, and leaves his palm flat on the warped board a moment longer than he needs to.

Then come the three questions. He answers them in order, one fact at a time.

"Salt's always gone out. A sack or two a year to dyers in the Gate, through Tull. Since before my time." He looks at the shelf. "Her boxes, sealed, that's new. Since the thaw. One a month. Two last month. This one's the third since midsummer."

"Not a carter." He thinks about it honestly before he answers. "Once. Back end of winter. Two men with a letter in Tull's hand. Walked the yard, counted the sheds. Asked how far down the water goes at the low end, and could it be pumped." His jaw shifts. "Didn't go down. I didn't offer. Good boots. They paid the carter in Amn silver for the ride up, Hob said. He bit it."

"The page." He taps the closed book once with a knuckle. "Tull gets a fair copy every quarter. Wages, tools, deaths, all of it. Whether he reads it, ask him." He shrugs one shoulder. "Up here nobody reads."

Pell gets up slowly, tries the shin and gets his pack onto his shoulders. He says what he'll do, and that Osric can hold him to it at the Red Sheaf: the case into Thorn's hands, the letter, her face when she reads *Vandarren*, and a careful question about what an apothecary wants with dye from a drowned gallery where men fall asleep. Last of all he says Tobin's name is Osric's, and he won't say it to anyone.

Osric hears that last part with his eyes on the fire, and nods once.

At the door Pell gives him his own advice back, dry as the dust: keep off the low end, nobody alone.

"Nobody here to be alone with." It's nearly a joke, the first one out of him. It goes as soon as it came. "Leave the blanket on. Hob can bring it back."

Outside the glare is waiting. The hemp rope still lies coiled by the iron ring in the cut face, the pinch-bar lies on the crust at the rim of the hole, and a thin cold breath comes up out of the hole into the sun. The sun is still well short of noon. The track down to the Way is the same one you came up, and there's half a day of road and daylight to spare.

*(Out of game: Sefa's offer to look at Pell's leg is still open for Pell's player to answer.)*

At the door Pell gives him his own advice back, dry as the dust: keep off the low end, nobody alone.

"Nobody here to be alone with." It's nearly a joke, the first one out of him. It goes as soon as it came. "Leave the blanket on. Hob can bring it back."

Outside the glare is waiting. The hemp rope still lies coiled by the iron ring in the cut face, the pinch-bar lies on the crust at the rim of the hole, and a thin cold breath comes up out of the hole into the sun. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps out into the white glare and lets the door close behind them. She settles her pack, touches the pouch at her belt once to be sure Osric's letter is still there, and looks from Bram to Pell.

"Then we go now, while the road's still warm and the sun's well up. I'll keep the letter, and I'll put it in Thorn's hand myself. Bram, the case stays with you. Pell, you say the word the moment that leg starts lying to you."

She falls in on the track beside Pell, close enough to take his weight if he sways, far enough not to hover. To the yard and the silent hole behind them, she gives one last look, but not a long one.

"The road first. The rest later, around a table, with food in front of us."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell stops at the hole on the way past. Not at the edge — two strides off it, on the grey rock Hale showed them. He picks up the pinch-bar, carries it back to lean against the house wall by the door, and coils Bram's hemp off the iron ring as he goes, handing it to him without a word. Then he looks down the shaft once, at the cold breath coming up, and turns his back on it.*

"Amn silver," *he says, low, once they're past the yard and onto the track proper.* "Two men with Tull's letter, asking if the low end can be pumped. Then the boxes start. One a month, then two." *He tugs the grey blanket tighter over his pack straps; he's still white to the collar and walking like a man with one leg a size too big.* "A patriar house stops its wardens' wages and a dyer in Beregost starts buying sealed cases of the stuff that killed Tobin — sorry. That killed a cutter. Within the same season." *He shakes his head.* "I don't believe in that kind of luck, and I was raised by a goddess of it."

*He drops back to his thirty paces, eyes on the ground, bruised shin dragging a little in the dust.*

"Sefa, you're right, it waits for a table. But when we get to Thorn's — let me give her the letter, not you. I want to see her read *Vandarren* before she knows we know the word. If she's just an apothecary who got a good price, she'll be puzzled. If she's not, she'll be quick." *A beat.* "Bram, if she's quick, don't let go of the case till the ninety's on the counter. Then let go of it. We're not thieves today."

*And then, because the sun's climbing and the road is long and the cold's finally starting to leave him, quieter, mostly to himself:*

"Glass face. Glows on its own. Men fall asleep. Someone wants it pumped dry." *He spits chalk.* "Nobody alone, Hale said. Aye. Nobody."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Mark that broken stretch before anyone else comes up, Hale. A cart won’t hear a warning.”

I recover my hemp rope from the ring on the solid rock and coil it onto my pack, leaving the pinch-bar rather than venturing onto the crust again.

Before we leave, I ask Osric to point out a safe way past the collapse to the track below. Then I take the lead, setting a pace Pell’s leg can manage.

“Give a word if that shin worsens,” I tell him. “We’ve daylight enough to walk sensibly. No prize for arriving on your face.”

scenes.narration:
Sefa steps out into the white glare, and the door swings shut behind her on the smell of woodsmoke. She shrugs her pack straight and touches the pouch at her belt once. The letter is there, folded twice, the warden's ink gone stiff in the last stroke. She says it plainly to both men: the road now, while the sun's well up. The letter stays with her and goes into Thorn's hand, the case stays with Bram, and Pell is to say the moment the leg starts lying to him. Then she falls in at Pell's side, close enough to catch him and not so close that she hovers. She gives the yard and the hole one look over her shoulder, a short one.

Pell stops by the hole on the way past, on the grey rock where Osric stamped. He keeps two strides back from the bad ground. From there he can see the pinch-bar lying where Bram left it, flat along the ragged rim on the white crust, about ten feet past the edge of the rock. It's too far to reach from where he stands. Cold air breathes up past it out of the shaft. The hemp is closer. He pulls it back through the iron ring in the face, hand over hand, wet and gritty, coils it in loops over his forearm and holds it out to Bram without a word. Bram takes it and lashes the coil to the top of his pack, above the bedroll-less space where the case sits dry in the bottom.

Osric is back in his doorway. He sees Pell looking at the bar.

"Leave it. I've a hook-pole." He tips his chin at the crust, and that's the end of it.

Bram turns to him across the yard. *Mark that broken stretch before anyone else comes up, a cart won't hear a warning.* Then he asks for a safe way past the collapse.

"Stakes and a rope across it. Today." Osric thinks about the second question before he answers it. "Face side. Keep your hand on the stone. Rock runs on under the dust past the hole, two strides wide. Where the spoil stops at the bend, it's track on rock again, all the way down." A pause. "No cart's coming up till there's coin. But I'll stake it."

He doesn't wave. He stands with his arms folded and the grey thread of his chimney going up behind him, and watches them go.

Bram goes first along the cut face with one palm on the white stone, testing every step with his heel, and the ground answers him with a dull solid knock each time. Sefa and Pell follow in his steps. Past the bend the white skin of spoil thins to nothing and the track is honest rock again, pale and rutted, winding down off the hill.

Once they're on the track proper, Pell talks low. He puts it together for the other two: the Amn silver, the two men with Tull's letter asking whether the low end could be pumped, then the boxes, one a month and then two, and wages stopped in the same season. He starts a name, catches it, and says *a cutter* instead. Then he says his piece about Thorn and the letter: he wants to be the one to hand it over, so he can watch her read *Vandarren* before she knows they know the word. To Bram he says that if she's quick about it, he's to keep hold of the case until the ninety is on the counter, and then let go of it. Then he drops back to his thirty paces, eyes on the dust, the grey blanket pulled tight over his straps.

Bram sets a pace the bruised shin can keep. *No prize for arriving on your face.*

The track comes down out of the hills the way they came up it in the dark, but by day it's a different road. It runs through scrub oak and gorse, over dry stream-beds, past a shepherd's fold with no shepherd in it. The sun climbs. Pell's clothes steam, then stiffen, then dry, with chalk cracking off them in flakes at the elbows and knees. The shaking leaves him somewhere in the second hour. The shin doesn't. It goes stiff whenever they stop, and by the third hour he's walking like a man with one boot nailed on. But it holds, every step of it.

A little after noon the track tops the last rise, and the Trade Way lies below them. It's a broad brown ribbon running north and south through pasture and hedges. Far up it to the north, a smudge of forge smoke marks Beregost, a good three hours off at this pace. The sun is high and well short of turning. There's time in hand.

Bram stands on the crest and looks the country over, because he has looked at this country for ten years.

He knows the hollow before he's properly looking for it. It's south of where the track meets the Way, about a mile off the road on the east side: a fold in the pasture with a stand of alders and a spring at the bottom. Caravans pull off into it when they're running late for Beregost or the inns are full. He's slept there himself more than once, with the wagons drawn round and the fire under the bank. The old ruts still turn off the Way toward it. They're greener than they ought to be, as if fewer wheels have used them lately.

There's a ring of stones in the hollow, a windbreak, the kind teamsters pile against the night wind. Inside it, on the grass, dark shapes lie in rows. They're too regular for stones and too flat for men. There are no wagons and no animals, and no smoke. A few crows walk among the shapes, unhurried, and nothing chases them off.

From up here that's all there is to see. It's a mile off the road and a mile back, with the afternoon still ahead of them.

Bram, you're at the front and you know that hollow. What do you do?

*(Out of game: Pell can't reach the pinch-bar from the rock. It lies on the crust about ten feet past the edge, so it's still at the rim where Bram left it, and Osric says he'll fish it out with his hook-pole.)*

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) Sefa keeps the letter in the pouch at her belt. Handing it to Thorn happens when you reach the shop, and Pell has asked to be the one who gives it, so that's Sefa's player's call first.

2) Pell pulled the hemp out of the ring and handed it to Bram, as the turn told. The pinch-bar is about ten feet out on the crust, past where he can reach from the rock, and Osric said aloud to leave it because he has a hook-pole. Pell's player answers that next round.

3) The letter is in Sefa's pouch, not Pell's, and you aren't at Thorn's yet. Whether Pell gives it to her is Sefa's player's answer to his request.

*He drops back to his thirty paces, eyes on the ground, bruised shin dragging a little in the dust.*

"Sefa, you're right, it waits for a table. But when we get to Thorn's — let me give her the letter, not you. I want to see her read *Vandarren* before she knows we know the word. If she's just an apothecary who got a good price, she'll be puzzled. If she's not, she'll be quick." *A beat.* "Bram, if she's quick, don't let go of the case till the ninety's on the counter. Then let go of it. We're not thieves today."

*And then, because the sun's climbing and the road is long and the cold's finally starting to leave him, quieter, mostly to himself:*

"Glass face. Glows on its own. Men fall asleep. Someone wants it pumped dry." *He spits chalk.* "Nobody alone, Hale said. Aye. Nobody."

Bram Halloway: “Mark that broken stretch before anyone else comes up, Hale. A cart won’t hear a warning.”

I recover my hemp rope from the ring on the solid rock and coil it onto my pack, leaving the pinch-bar rather than venturing onto the crust again.

Before we leave, I ask Osric to point out a safe way past the collapse to the track below. Then I take the lead, setting a pace Pell’s leg can manage.

“Give a word if that shin worsens,” I tell him. “We’ve daylight enough to walk sensibly. No prize for arriving on your face.”

Your narration:
<<<
Sefa steps out into the white glare, and the door swings shut behind her on the smell of woodsmoke. She shrugs her pack straight and touches the pouch at her belt once. The letter is there, folded twice, the warden's ink gone stiff in the last stroke. She says it plainly to both men: the road now, while the sun's well up. The letter stays with her and goes into Thorn's hand, the case stays with Bram, and Pell is to say the moment the leg starts lying to him. Then she falls in at Pell's side, close enough to catch him and not so close that she hovers. She gives the yard and the hole one look over her shoulder, a short one.

Pell stops by the hole on the way past, on the grey rock where Osric stamped. He keeps two strides back from the bad ground. From there he can see the pinch-bar lying where Bram left it, flat along the ragged rim on the white crust, about ten feet past the edge of the rock. It's too far to reach from where he stands. Cold air breathes up past it out of the shaft. The hemp is closer. He pulls it back through the iron ring in the face, hand over hand, wet and gritty, coils it in loops over his forearm and holds it out to Bram without a word. Bram takes it and lashes the coil to the top of his pack, above the bedroll-less space where the case sits dry in the bottom.

Osric is back in his doorway. He sees Pell looking at the bar.

"Leave it. I've a hook-pole." He tips his chin at the crust, and that's the end of it.

Bram turns to him across the yard. *Mark that broken stretch before anyone else comes up, a cart won't hear a warning.* Then he asks for a safe way past the collapse.

"Stakes and a rope across it. Today." Osric thinks about the second question before he answers it. "Face side. Keep your hand on the stone. Rock runs on under the dust past the hole, two strides wide. Where the spoil stops at the bend, it's track on rock again, all the way down." A pause. "No cart's coming up till there's coin. But I'll stake it."

He doesn't wave. He stands with his arms folded and the grey thread of his chimney going up behind him, and watches them go.

Bram goes first along the cut face with one palm on the white stone, testing every step with his heel, and the ground answers him with a dull solid knock each time. Sefa and Pell follow in his steps. Past the bend the white skin of spoil thins to nothing and the track is honest rock again, pale and rutted, winding down off the hill.

Once they're on the track proper, Pell talks low. He puts it together for the other two: the Amn silver, the two men with Tull's letter asking whether the low end could be pumped, then the boxes, one a month and then two, and wages stopped in the same season. He starts a name, catches it, and says *a cutter* instead. Then he says his piece about Thorn and the letter: he wants to be the one to hand it over, so he can watch her read *Vandarren* before she knows they know the word. To Bram he says that if she's quick about it, he's to keep hold of the case until the ninety is on the counter, and then let go of it. Then he drops back to his thirty paces, eyes on the dust, the grey blanket pulled tight over his straps.

Bram sets a pace the bruised shin can keep. *No prize for arriving on your face.*

The track comes down out of the hills the way they came up it in the dark, but by day it's a different road. It runs through scrub oak and gorse, over dry stream-beds, past a shepherd's fold with no shepherd in it. The sun climbs. Pell's clothes steam, then stiffen, then dry, with chalk cracking off them in flakes at the elbows and knees. The shaking leaves him somewhere in the second hour. The shin doesn't. It goes stiff whenever they stop, and by the third hour he's walking like a man with one boot nailed on. But it holds, every step of it.

A little after noon the track tops the last rise, and the Trade Way lies below them. It's a broad brown ribbon running north and south through pasture and hedges. Far up it to the north, a smudge of forge smoke marks Beregost, a good three hours off at this pace. The sun is high and well short of turning. There's time in hand.

Bram stands on the crest and looks the country over, because he has looked at this country for ten years.

He knows the hollow before he's properly looking for it. It's south of where the track meets the Way, about a mile off the road on the east side: a fold in the pasture with a stand of alders and a spring at the bottom. Caravans pull off into it when they're running late for Beregost or the inns are full. He's slept there himself more than once, with the wagons drawn round and the fire under the bank. The old ruts still turn off the Way toward it. They're greener than they ought to be, as if fewer wheels have used them lately.

There's a ring of stones in the hollow, a windbreak, the kind teamsters pile against the night wind. Inside it, on the grass, dark shapes lie in rows. They're too regular for stones and too flat for men. There are no wagons and no animals, and no smoke. A few crows walk among the shapes, unhurried, and nothing chases them off.

From up here that's all there is to see. It's a mile off the road and a mile back, with the afternoon still ahead of them.

Bram, you're at the front and you know that hollow. What do you do?

1) Sefa keeps the letter in the pouch at her belt. Handing it to Thorn happens when you reach the shop, and Pell has asked to be the one who gives it, so that's Sefa's player's call first.

2) Pell pulled the hemp out of the ring and handed it to Bram, as the turn told. The pinch-bar is about ten feet out on the crust, past where he can reach from the rock, and Osric said aloud to leave it because he has a hook-pole. Pell's player answers that next round.

3) The letter is in Sefa's pouch, not Pell's, and you aren't at Thorn's yet. Whether Pell gives it to her is Sefa's player's answer to his request.

journal: Thread: The Empty Camp in Alder Hollow

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell comes up the last of the rise slower than he'd like and stops a pace behind Bram, hands on his knees for a breath. Then he follows the big man's eyes south, shading his own against the glare.*

"What've you got?" *He squints at the hollow — the alders, the dark line of the spring, anything that doesn't belong in a shepherd's country: a cart, a mule, a fire-scar, a shape that lies the wrong way.* "Say it before you point. I'd rather know what you think it is than look for it."

*He straightens, hand going to the small of his back, and glances north at the forge smoke and then up at the sun.*

"Three hours to Beregost, four with my leg. Sunset's the better part of six away. So we've slack — some. But a mile off the road and a mile back is an hour we don't get again, and that's before anyone in that hollow has opinions about us." *A dry look at Bram's pack.* "And we're carrying the only coin on the hill. I'd sooner not carry it into somebody's camp."

*A beat. The roof-runner in him is already measuring the ground between here and the alders — hedgerows, dead ground, where a man could get close without being seen from the spring.*

"If it's nothing — a drover's fire, a few sheep — we walk on and I'll owe you a look. If it's a camp with no one in it, in a hollow a mile off the Way, the day after a quarry's men walked down this same road..." *He doesn't finish.* "Then one of us goes and looks, and it's me, because I'm the one who can do it without being seen. From the hedge line, not from the middle of it. Ten minutes, no more, and I'm not going in alone — Sefa, you'd stay at the hedge where you can see me and I can see you. Nobody alone. I'm told that's the rule today."

*He waits on Bram's answer — he gave the man the lead and means to keep to it.*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stop and point out the hollow to the others.

“Caravan camp. Good spring, shelter under the bank. I’ve slept there. Those rows are new—and there ought to be wagons if someone’s using it.”

I study the shapes from the rise, shading my eyes, looking for movement or anything I recognise as clothing, bedrolls or discarded harness.

“That’s two miles extra to look properly, with Pell limping. Unless we see someone needing help, I say we keep for Beregost and report it. But have a look before we move.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa comes up even with Bram and follows his gaze down to the hollow. The crows walking among the shapes settle something cold in her stomach, the same cold that came up out of the hole at Whitestone.

"What is it, Bram? You've gone still as a man counting." She keeps her voice low, though there's no one but the crows to hear. "Rows and a ring of stones — it could be drovers, or it could be what's left of them. Do we look, or do we keep to the Way and note it for the Fist or the temple?"

She shifts her pack and glances over her shoulder for Pell, still pacing along behind them.

"I've light and a steadying hand for the dead, if that's what's down there. But I won't walk us off the road into an ambush for the sake of a look."

scenes.narration:
Bram is still for a long moment on the crest, the way a man is when he's working out what a thing is before he says it.

Bram is still for a long moment on the crest, a hand flat over his eyes against the glare. He's working out what the thing is before he says it, the way Pell asked him to.

Bram reads it the way he'd read any camp he was riding into. **His eyes find the detail a mile off and hold it.** The dark shapes are bedrolls. There are twenty or more of them, laid out in rows inside the windbreak with their feet toward the middle, the way a caravan beds down round its fire. In the middle of the ring is a round black scar where the fire was. The bedrolls are spread out flat, not rolled and not slept in. They're a dull grey-brown, sunk into the grass the way cloth goes after rain and sun and more rain. That takes weeks, not days. The crows walk between the rows and stab at the ground, at spilled meal or whatever's left of somebody's rations.

He can also see what isn't there. No wagon stands in the hollow and none has been burned in it. There are no mule carcasses, no dropped harness, no gap kicked in the windbreak where men broke out, and nothing scattered. At the mouth of the hollow the grass lies pressed in two broad, pale stripes. Wagons went out that way onto the Way, heading south, a long time ago. Ten years on this road have taught him how a camp looks after it fights: gear everywhere, a cart on its side, a dead animal, something torn. A camp that breaks up and moves on rolls its beds. This one did neither. Its people lay down, and their beds are still lying there.

Beside him Pell shades his eyes and looks hard, and **the glare beats him**. The pasture swims white-green, the alders are a dark smudge, and the rows are only shapes with crows among them. From here he can't tell one thing from another.

The ground between here and the hollow is another matter. That's his trade, and he reads it without trying. A hawthorn hedge follows the old ruts down from the Way almost to the alders, a little higher than a man, and solid enough to walk behind unseen from the spring. Where the hedge stops there's about a hundred feet of open grass before the windbreak, and no cover on it at all. The alders are thick round the spring. Anyone sitting in them could watch the whole of that hundred feet, and nobody on the grass could see in.

Sefa sees what anyone could see from the rise: the ring, the rows and the crows. Nothing moves down there except the birds. No smoke, no voice carries up, and nobody calls out for help.

North, the forge smoke over Beregost stands up straight in the still air. The sun is a little past noon.

*(Out of game: Bram can tell the others what he saw, in his own words. Pell's plan, the hedge with Sefa watching and ten minutes, and Bram's plan, Beregost and a report, are both still on the table. Sefa, Pell asked you to keep the hedge with him if anyone goes down.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Beds,” I say. “Twenty or more, laid round the fire. Been weathering there for weeks. Wagons left south. No wrecks, no scattered harness, no sign of a fight. But nobody packed their bedding.”

I point out the bare stretch before the windbreak. “And anyone in those alders could watch you cross that.”

I turn to Pell. “Not yesterday’s quarry lads. And not ten minutes on that leg. I’d look if we weren’t carrying someone’s goods against a deadline—but this has waited weeks.”

“Let’s deliver the case, report exactly what we’ve seen, and ask whether a caravan’s missing. Then we can come back with daylight and sound legs, rather than creep in half-ready.”

I take a last look to fix the place in memory, then turn toward Beregost, keeping our pace manageable for Pell.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays a step back from the crest edge, reading the same signs: no smoke, no stirring, no voice. Just crows and the patient work of birds.

"We'll do no one any good if we come into Beregost after sunset, and we won't carry a warning faster by being dead or limping. If that was a man calling for help, we'd have heard something. It's still as a grave."

She looks to Pell, not unkindly. "I'll not stop you taking ten minutes from the hedge, if your leg swears to it and you keep within my sight. But I say it with Bram: unless you find someone living down there, we don't touch it or linger. We mark it, we mention it to the right ear in town. Thorn first, case in hand, and then the Red Sheaf already knows men from Whitestone."

She shifts her pack and turns toward the Trade Way. "If you go, go now. We'll wait on the road, not on the hill. And if a single crow lifts off differently, you come back at a run — or as near to it as that shin allows."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell lowers his hand and blinks the glare out of his eyes.*

"Sun's beating me. All I've got from here is crows and shapes, and crows don't settle on drovers who are only sleeping." *He glances at Bram.* "You've slept there. You know what the rows ought to look like. I'll take your read over mine."

*He nods down at the ground between them and the alders.*

"But the approach I can tell you. That hawthorn hedge follows the old ruts nearly to the trees — higher than a man, thick enough to walk behind without the spring seeing you. Then it stops, and there's a hundred feet of bare grass before the alders, and anyone sat in those trees owns every inch of it. Nobody crosses that grass without being seen. So nobody crosses it."

*He shifts his weight off the bad shin.*

"Here's the cheap version, if you want one. I go down behind the hedge to where it ends — that's half a mile, not a mile, and it's cover the whole way. I don't step onto the grass. From the hedge end I'll be close enough to see what the rows are and whether anything in the alders is breathing. Sefa comes to the hedge with me and stays where she can see both me and you; you hold the crest with the case and a view of the road both ways. If I see a reason to go further, I come back and say so first. If I see bodies and nothing else, we've a tale for the Fist that's worth something, and we've lost half an hour, not two."

*A beat.* "And if you'd rather walk on and tell Beregost — say it, and I'll walk. The case is the job. I'm only offering because I'd hate to find out tomorrow that someone down there was alive at noon."

*He waits on Bram.*

Bram says it plainly, the way he'd report to a caravan master: beds, twenty or more, laid round the fire and left weathering for weeks. The wagons went out south. There are no wrecks, no scattered harness and no sign of a fight, but nobody packed their bedding. He points down at the bare grass between the hedge-end and the windbreak. *Anyone in those alders could watch you cross that.* Then he turns to Pell. These aren't yesterday's quarry lads, and it isn't ten minutes on that leg. Deliver the case first, report exactly what they saw, ask whether a caravan's missing, and come back by daylight on sound legs.

He takes his last look before he turns, and for a man who has driven this stretch for ten years it's an easy place to fix. The old ruts leave the Way beside a stunted ash with a split crown, the only tree on that side of the road for a long way. The hedge runs east from there. The hollow sits under the second fold of the pasture, where a ribbon of the spring shows silver for a moment between the alders. He could walk a Fist sergeant straight to it in the dark.

Sefa stays a step back from the edge and reads what anyone could read: no smoke, nothing moving, no voice, only crows going about their business. She says her piece. If someone down there were calling for help they'd have heard it, and nobody carries a warning faster by arriving dead or limping after sunset. Pell can have his look from the hedge if his leg swears to it and he stays in her sight, but unless he finds someone alive they touch nothing and don't linger. Then she settles her pack and starts down toward the Way. *If you go, go now. We'll wait on the road, not on the hill.*

Pell blinks the glare out of his eyes and gives Bram the read, since Bram is the one who has slept down there. Then he gives them the ground, because that part is his: the hedge offers cover all the way to its end, the last hundred feet are open grass that nobody crosses, and the cheap version is half a mile behind the hedge to where it stops, with no step onto the grass. Pell is only offering because he'd hate to learn tomorrow that someone down there was alive at noon.

Nothing has changed down in the hollow. A crow lifts, flaps a few lazy beats over the windbreak and drops again a row further on. On the Way below, a single ox-cart creaks north toward Beregost, piled with hurdles. Its driver is asleep on the seat with his hat over his face, and the ox seems to know the road without him. The forge smoke stands straight over the town. The sun has barely moved off noon.

Bram has already turned his shoulder toward Beregost. Sefa is a dozen steps down the slope toward the road. Pell stands on the crest with the hedge-line below him and his weight off the bad shin.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops on the slope, turns halfway, and looks up at Pell. She doesn't frown.

"I'll not let you go alone — not today, and not on that leg. So if there's to be a look, it's a party-line look, and it costs ten minutes at the hedge end, no open ground, nobody out of anyone's sight."

She glances at Bram, then back at Pell, calm.

"Bram's read says dead camp or cold camp, but we've no proof it's neither, and we'd not like telling it in Beregost that we walked past a man too hurt to call. So: as far as the hedge runs, eyes on the hollow, see if a boot stirs or a bird flushes round something living. If it's only crows, we turn for the Way and keep Thorn's sunset in front of us."

She sets her shoulders under the pack and starts back up the dozen steps, not quickly.

"Ten minutes, Pell. And if that hedge lies — if the ground's worse than you say — we walk away with the truth of it and mark it for the Fist."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
*Pell looks at the hollow a moment longer. Then at the crow settling a row further on. Then at Bram's back, already turned north.*

"Aye. You said it, I'll walk it."

*He comes down off the crest after them, favouring the shin, and falls in — not thirty paces back this time but at Sefa's shoulder, where he can be caught if the leg goes.*

"Weeks, you said. Twenty beds, wagons gone south, nobody took their blankets." *He says it to keep it, the way he kept Tobin's name.* "That's not drovers. Drovers don't own twenty bedrolls and a caravan master doesn't leave them to the weather. That's a camp someone walked out of at night and didn't come back to — or was walked out of." *A glance south, at the alders dropping behind the rise.* "Guards and all. There's been talk at the Friendly Arm since spring, if you believe the Arm."

*He pulls the grey blanket straight over his pack.*

"Right. Beregost. Case first, ninety on the counter, letter in Thorn's hand — mine, Sefa, if you'll let me, for the reason I gave. Then the Red Sheaf for Hob Carrow and the round I owe you both. And somewhere in between, a Fist sergeant or a Lathander priest who'll hear 'Alder Hollow, twenty beds, weeks old, wagons went south' and know whether a caravan's gone missing." *Dry:* "We'll tell them we didn't go down. They'll like us for it. Nobody ever likes the ones who went down."

*He sets his jaw against the shin and matches Bram's pace.*

"And Bram — if we do come back by daylight on sound legs, I'm the one who goes to the hedge end. Just so it's said now, while I can't argue about it."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’d rather we walk on, Pell. Can’t swear there’s nobody alive there, but I’ve seen no sign of it. That’s not enough to send you down on a bad leg while we split three ways.”

I join Sefa on the road and wait for Pell to come alongside.

As we approach the ox-cart, I call from beside the road, well clear of the animal. “Ho, driver! Heading to Beregost? Could you spare a seat for a man with a hurt leg?”

If he wakes, I also ask, “Passed the alder hollow lately? There’s a camp’s bedding abandoned out there. Wondered if you’d heard what happened.”

scenes.narration:
Sefa turns on the slope a dozen steps down and climbs back toward the crest, unhurried, saying her piece as she goes: if anyone looks, they all go, ten minutes at the hedge end, nobody out of sight, and back to the Way if it's only crows.

She's halfway up when Pell starts down off the crest toward her, favouring the shin. *Aye. You said it, I'll walk it.* That's for Bram, and Bram is already walking. Pell doesn't drop back to thirty paces this time. He falls in at Sefa's shoulder, close enough to be caught if the leg goes, and goes over it aloud so he'll keep it: twenty beds left out for weeks, the wagons gone south, nobody took their blankets. Drovers don't own twenty bedrolls, and a caravan master doesn't leave them out to the weather. Then he lays out the plan: Beregost, the case, the ninety on the counter, the letter in Thorn's hand. He wants to give it himself, *if you'll let me, Sefa.* After that the Red Sheaf, and somewhere along the way a Fist sergeant or a priest who'll know whether a caravan is missing. Last of all, so it's said while he can't argue: if they ever come back, he's the one who goes to the hedge end.

Bram doesn't stop to argue it again. *I'd rather we walk on.* He has seen no sign of anyone alive, and that isn't enough to send a man down on a bad leg. He goes down the last of the slope onto the Way and waits on the verge for the other two.

The ox-cart hasn't got far. It's ahead of them on the brown road, going north at the speed of an animal that has decided the whole day is its own. It's a two-wheeled thing, piled shoulder-high with woven hazel hurdles roped down in a stack. The driver is still asleep on the seat with his hat over his face, one boot up on the shaft.

Bram stays well clear of the ox and calls out in his road voice: "Ho, driver!"

She sets her shoulders under the pack and starts back up the dozen steps, not quickly.

"Ten minutes, Pell. And if that hedge lies — if the ground's worse than you say — we walk away with the truth of it and mark it for the Fist."

"Aye. You said it, I'll walk it."

*He comes down off the crest after them, favouring the shin, and falls in — not thirty paces back this time but at Sefa's shoulder, where he can be caught if the leg goes.*

There's been talk at the Friendly Arm since spring, if you believe the Arm."

*He pulls the grey blanket straight over his pack.*

"Right. Beregost. Case first, ninety on the counter, letter in Thorn's hand — mine, Sefa, if you'll let me, for the reason I gave. Then the Red Sheaf for Hob Carrow and the round I owe you both. They'll like us for it. Nobody ever likes the ones who went down."

*He sets his jaw against the shin and matches Bram's pace.*

"And Bram — if we do come back by daylight on sound legs, I'm the one who goes to the hedge end. Just so it's said now, while I can't argue about it."

I join Sefa on the road and wait for Pell to come alongside.

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.
