private.text:
Pell labours up the final stretch of the rise, slower than he would like, and halts just behind you, bent over with his hands braced on his knees to catch his breath. He follows your gaze south, shading his eyes against the glare. He asks what you see, and wants to hear what you think it is before you point it out. Then he reckons the day aloud: three hours to Beregost, four with his bad leg, and sunset about six hours off. That leaves some slack, but a detour of a mile out and a mile back costs an hour you won't get again, and you are carrying the only coin on the hill. If it's only a drover's fire, he says, you walk on. If it's an empty camp a mile from the Way, the day after the men of a quarry came down this same road, he lets the thought trail off. Then one of you should look, and he says it should be him, since he can get close unseen. He would work from the hedge line and take ten minutes at most. He won't go in alone: Sefa would stay at the hedge where they can see each other, because the rule today is that nobody goes alone. He waits on your answer.

Sefa comes up level with you and looks down at the hollow. Quietly, she says you've gone as still as a man counting, and asks what it is. She points out the rows and the ring of stones, and says it could be drovers, or what's left of them. She asks whether you look, or keep to the Way and report it to the Fist or the temple. She says she has light and a steady hand for the dead if that's what lies down there, but she won't walk the three of you into an ambush just for a look. She glances back for Pell.

You stand still on the crest for a long moment, working out what the thing below is before you say it.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Sefa Marrin — Human, warlock 5 (The Celestial — the Lantern; Pact of the Tome), former hospice novice, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 14 · Speed 30 feet
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 18
Skills: Persuasion +7; Arcana +4; Religion +4; Insight +3
Saves: Wisdom saving throw +3 (proficient); Charisma saving throw +7 (proficient); Strength saving throw −1; Dexterity saving throw +2; Constitution saving throw +2; Intelligence saving throw +1
Attacks: Eldritch Blast +7 to hit, two beams, 1d10+4 force each, range 120 feet; Dagger +5 to hit, 1d4+2 piercing, thrown 20/60
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Spell attack +7; spell save DC 15; Pact Magic: two 3rd-level pact slots, recovered only on a short or long rest; Healing Light: a pool of six d6 per long rest; a bonus action spends up to four dice to heal a creature within 60 feet; Pact of the Tome: the Book of Shadows holds three extra cantrips (Guidance, Spare the Dying, Thaumaturgy); Agonizing Blast: +4 to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Repelling Blast: a beam that hits pushes the target up to 10 feet away; Eyes of the Rune Keeper: reads all writing
Spells: Eldritch Blast (cantrip); Light (cantrip); Sacred Flame (cantrip); Mage Hand (cantrip); Minor Illusion (cantrip); Guidance (cantrip); Spare the Dying (cantrip); Thaumaturgy (cantrip); Cure Wounds (1); Guiding Bolt (1); Misty Step (2); Lesser Restoration (2); Hold Person (2); Daylight (3)
Limits: Two pact slots only, back only after a rest; Light armour; Strength 8 — weak up close; One concentration spell at a time
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Pact slots 2/2; Healing light 6/6; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 1 pp; 8 gp; 41 sp; 12 cp
Worn: Amulet: Prayer Beads; Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Book of Shadows; Main hand: Dagger
Pack: Bedroll and Rations; Candle ×2; Tinderbox

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell slows a step and lets Bram walk ahead on the track. His eyes travel over the sheds, the heaps of spoil, the lifting frame and the half-loaded cart with no mule. He says low, without turning his head, that the tools were left where the men were working and the cart abandoned mid-load, and that no one leaves a wage like that just to eat. He tells Bram to do the talking and says he'll watch the sheds, and he asks you to stay between them. He keeps his hands loose and visible, away from his shortsword, and looks over the yard as you come on. Near the warden he asks, friendly and plain, whether the day has been quiet, and says Maela Thorn sent you for the case.

Bram murmurs that it's quiet for a working quarry, then walks up to the house at an easy pace, sword sheathed and shield held low. He stops a few paces from the man to give him room. He gives his name, says Maela Thorn sent you for her sealed case of dye-salts, and asks if the man is the warden. He glances back at the abandoned cart and asks whether everyone stopped for something.

The quarry is just as quiet up close. White dust lies over everything in a soft skin.

The man in the doorway lets you come. He looks at each of you in turn, the big one first. Up close he's in his fifties, grey-bearded, with white dust in the creases of his knuckles and his apron. The keys at his belt are old iron, a dozen of them.

"Hale. Osric Hale. I'm the warden." His voice is gravel, and he uses no more of it than he has to. He tips his chin at the cart. "They stopped for pay. Noon bell, yesterday. Three weeks of none, and they walked." He doesn't sound angry about it. "I'd have walked too, if it was my back."

Then he looks at you, because you named the salts. "The case is inside. Sealed, like she wants it." He doesn't step out of the doorway. "Thorn's bought it. So she's paid someone. Not me, and not them." He nods at the empty track. "Before it leaves my house, I'll hear who she paid. And whether she knows where my men's wages went."

He waits with his arms folded, his eyes on Bram, as if the big man in mail is the one who'll answer for all three.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, a few paces from the warden's doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

You keep your hands open and tell the warden that Thorn pays ninety gold for the walk and the carrying, nothing until the case is in her shop by sunset, and that you knew nothing of missing wages. You offer to take what's under her seal and carry his complaint back, or, if he keeps you, Thorn will say the case never came.

Bram had spoken first, agreeing that three weeks unpaid is reason to stop. He kept his hands off his sword, said you are hired carriers who were never told who took Thorn's money, and asked who handles wages and who sold her the salts. He offered to carry a tally or letter but promised no answer.

Pell drifts back to Bram's shoulder and murmurs that the tracks agree with the warden: a dozen men and a single mule went down the road yesterday around noon, walking easy, with no one after them. Then he steps up to the warden and says that coin does not travel to a warden who has a dozen keys but no men, so whoever owns Whitestone holds the wages. He asks for the owner's name, offers to put it to Thorn's face tonight, and offers to carry a letter. He adds that if the case misses Beregost by sunset, no one is paid at all.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving. His hands stay folded, nowhere near the keys. When you say "keep us here", his jaw shifts, like a man told what he already knew. At Pell's words about the only coin on the hill, his eyes go toward the lower cut and come straight back.

"House Vandarren," Osric says. "Patriars, in the Gate. Whitestone's theirs on paper. Their factor's a man called Tull, in the Lower City. Coin comes up from Tull, I pay the lads. That's how it's gone for thirty years." Three weeks back it stopped, and he wrote four times with no answer.

He tells Bram the salts weren't sold by him: he cuts it, boxes it, seals it, and it goes. Somebody paid for it, and that's Tull, so that's Vandarren. Fourteen men are owed three weeks, fifty-odd gold, the carter most. They're in Beregost now, drinking what they had left. Not taken, not run off. Walked.

He unfolds his arms and steps out of the doorway. "Come in. Case is on the table."

The house is one long room, cool after the glare, with a hearth and kettle, a cot, shelves of damp-swollen ledgers and white dust everywhere. On a plank table under the window sits a case the size of a bread loaf, oak with iron corners, bound in waxed cord, a disc of red wax on the knot bearing Maela Thorn's mark. Beside it lie a pen, a thick ink-pot, and a sheet with three lines in a big cramped hand, two crossed out.

Osric stays standing. The case goes with you, he says, and a letter to Thorn with it; she can ask Tull where the rest went. He looks at the crossed-out lines, then at you, since you spoke for the money. "I cut stone. I don't write much." He pushes the pen an inch toward you. "You write a fair hand?"

The case sits on the table between you all, untouched.

Where you are: in the warden's house at Whitestone, by the table with the case · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell nods your way as you take the pen, then goes to the table himself. He looks the case over, cord, knot, wax and iron corners, tilts it an inch and sets it back where it was. He asks Osric if he may check the seal, saying he doubts the road, not the warden. Osric says to look, and stands while Pell does.

You turn the sheet toward you. The warden's three lines are in a big, cramped hand pressed hard into the paper. The first reads *To Mistress Thorn*. The second, crossed out, reads *The salt is paid for and my men are not*. The third, also crossed out, gets as far as *I have wrote to Tull four* and stops where the nib split.

Osric watches you test the nib. He thinks before he speaks, then gives you his words one at a time, like setting stones.

"To Mistress Thorn. The salt you bought is cut and sealed and sent." He waits for the pen. "You paid Tull. Tull is House Vandarren's factor in the Gate. None of that coin came to Whitestone." When you ask how to spell it, he says "Tull. Two l's," and when you read it back, "Vandarren. Like the mark on the deeds." He goes on. "Fourteen men, three weeks unpaid. Fifty gold and some. The carter's owed most. I have written to Tull four times. No answer. Ask him where it went. He'll answer a buyer." He stops, as if he's used up what he had.

You offer your last line. He looks at the sheet, not at you. "Put it." You write that the quarry stands silent and the men are in Beregost, unpaid. When you turn the paper to him, he takes the pen in his fist like a chisel and signs *O. Hale, Warden*, so hard the ink pools in the last stroke. He blows on it, folds it twice with his thumbnail and puts it in your hand. "Your hand wrote it. You give it to her."

Pell speaks low to Osric about the lower cut, and Osric answers him in a quiet voice: there is no strongbox and nobody of Tull's, nobody at all. The salt comes from old flooded workings below the lower cut, he says, growing rose-white on the walls like frost, scraped from a ledge. The ground is hollow under half the hill, some of it rotten. Keep to the track, and don't go poking at the low end. Then he falls silent and stands very still.

Pell also says the sun won't wait. He suggests Bram carry the case and that he himself will take the back on the road. Bram takes the case in hand and carries it easily under his shield arm. Osric tells him to keep it dry: damp, it cakes. That is all he knows of carrying it.

Both men ask where the workers are. Osric answers them together. "The Red Sheaf. Low end of Beregost, past the smithies. Cheapest ale on the Way." He tips his chin at the letter in your hand. "Carter's Hob Carrow. Red beard, one mule, a temper. If Thorn sends anything, give it to Hob. He'll share it out straight. He can't count crooked."

He looks round at the three of you, and something in his shoulders loosens a little.

"That's it, then. Track's the same one you came up."

The sun through the window has climbed past the frame. You have a half-day of road ahead, with time in hand before sunset.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Osric's Letter to Maela Thorn

Where you are: the warden's room at the Whitestone quarry, by the table · Time: Day 1 · morning

You tuck Osric's letter into a pouch at your belt, not into the Book of Shadows, and tell Osric you will see it into Thorn's hands with his words, and that if you find Hob Carrow you'll tell him what Osric said about the sharing. Osric answers only "Hob'll do it straight." Pell offered Osric word through Thorn's shop if the hollow ground ever troubled him, set out his plan for the road with a signal of one whistle for bored and two for trouble behind, and went out ahead of you into the glare. Bram wrapped the case in his bedroll in his pack, thanked Osric and told him to mind himself, and Osric answered "Always do." You said the case goes to Thorn first, and the Red Sheaf only if the road is kind and not at the cost of the sunset.

Outside, the glare is hard after the cool of the house. Bram checks that the flap of his pack covers the case, glances once at the sun and sets off down the track at a steady road pace. You follow a few steps behind him with the letter at your belt. Pell lets you both get ahead, thirty paces or so, and walks with his eyes on the ground.

Then you hear a crack like a plate breaking, then a crash and the slap of water. You turn to see a plume of white dust standing where Pell was. Thirty paces back along the lip of the cut there's a hole in the track the size of a cart bed, and no Pell.

In the doorway of the warden's house, Osric Hale's arms come unfolded.

"That's over the old third gallery," he calls down the yard, already walking, not running. "Don't stand at the edge. It goes in a ring."

The hole is in front of you and Osric is coming down the yard behind you. What do you do?

Where you are: on the track by the lower cut, near the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram called down the hole to Pell as well. He set his pack down well back from the collapse, then took out his rope and tied a loop in one end big enough to go over a man's shoulders. He asked Osric where the solid ground was and whether there was another way into the gallery, and told you to keep clear of the edge.

Dust still hangs over the hole in a slow white cloud and drifts off down the cut. Whatever answer comes up from below belongs to Pell.

Osric reaches you on the inner side of the track, against the cut face, and goes no nearer the hole than you have. He stamps his heel once, and the ground gives back a dull, solid knock, not the hollow sound the spoil made. "Here. This side." He scuffs the dust aside and grey rock shows underneath, smooth and old. "Living stone, from the face out about two strides. Past that it's spoil over timber, all the way round the hole. That's the ring." He nods toward the lip. "Edge'll take a man lying flat. Not standing."

Bram has already put his pack down well back on the rock, with the bedroll and the case inside it. He shakes out the hempen rope and ties a bowline in one end. Osric doesn't wait to be asked about an anchor. There's an iron ring set into the face about fifteen feet uphill of the hole, rusty but leaded deep into the rock. It was a guy-point for the lifting frame, back when the frame stood here. Bram hauls on it with his weight and it doesn't give. He runs the rope through it and takes a turn round his own waist. Now the line can go over the lip without anyone standing on it.

"Other way in?" Osric looks down the cut toward the foot of the lower face. "Old adit, down the bottom. Boarded. Water's to the lintel since before my time." He shakes his head once. "That hole's your way in."

Osric looks at you as you speak of the line, the light and then the hand, and he seems to agree with the order of it.

"There's a pinch-bar in the near shed. Iron. Longer than me." He is already turning toward it. "Get him out quick. Cold sits in you down there."

He goes off across the yard at his usual walking pace, but he doesn't fold his arms.

Bram stands at the anchor with the loop ready in his hand. The lip of the hole is about ten feet off across the bad ground, and he can lie flat on it or throw from where he is. You kneel two strides back on the living rock. Osric is at the near shed, dragging the door open.

Where you are: kneeling on solid rock two strides back from the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram throws the hempen loop down the hole from the solid rock and pays out rope so it can reach below instead of hanging tight across the opening. He calls down to Pell to get the loop under his arms if he can and to say when he's secure, and promises that nobody will haul until Pell is ready. He braces at the anchor and asks you whether you can get light down there.

You go down flat on the grey rock and work forward on your elbows. Two strides out, the living stone ends under you and the white crust begins. You feel the difference through your stays: rock, then something that gives a hair, like a mattress over boards. It creaks once, a dry creak deep down in the timber. It holds. Osric said it would hold a body lying flat, and it does. You stop an arm's length short of the ragged rim, put your fingers on the lump of chalk in your hand, and the Lantern's light wakes in it, clear and white, as bright as a hooded lantern with the shutter open. You hold it out over the drop at arm's length.

Your voice goes down the shaft clearly: can he see you, will he take the rope first if it reaches him, will he not try to climb until he's told you how he's lying, and will he answer twice for yes if he can't speak well. Pell's answer is not something you can pick out.

The light falls down the hole and the dark below opens up.

The gallery is lower than you'd pictured, the old roof barely a man's height above the water. The water is black and very still except round Pell. He's there, in it to the chest, soaked white with chalk on his hair and shoulders, his face pale against the dark. A coil of pale silk rope hangs over one of his arms. Bram's hempen loop floats a yard from him where it landed. Past him, a squared block of dressed stone lies under the surface. Its near edge shows as a straight pale line in the water. The rest of it is a shape, and the shape runs across where his left leg ought to be. Across the gallery an oak beam lies half-sunk, one end propped on the rubble. Along one wall something rose-white catches your light and glitters like frost on a pane.

At the far end of the block, where it meets the gallery wall, there's a seam of old grey plaster. As your light passes over it, the plaster seems to hold the light a breath longer than wet stone should. Then it's just plaster again. It could be the water throwing your light back. You're flat on your belly at the edge of a hole, and your arm is starting to shake.

Bram, back at the guy-ring, feeds out slack until the hempen line lies loose over the lip. He keeps the turn round his waist and doesn't pull.

Boots come across the yard behind you, steady, and something iron scrapes on stone. Osric comes back along the cut face with the pinch-bar on his shoulder, black iron, longer than he is, one end flattened into a chisel lip. He stops on the living rock next to Bram, looks down the line, then at you lying on the crust with your light held out.

"Don't haul him," he says. "Leg's under it. Pull now and you leave the leg." He stands the bar on its foot. "Block first. Bar goes in under the near edge from the lip, lying down. His rope off the block comes up to whoever's on the ring. Bar lifts, rope rolls it. Two of you, few minutes." His voice drops. "He's been in that cold long enough."

He holds the bar out across the gap toward Bram, handle first, without stepping onto the crust. "You've the weight for the bar. I'll take the ring." Then, to you, without turning his head: "Keep that light where it is. Can you hold it and him both talking?"

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Lit Lump of Chalk

Where you are: lying flat on the white crust at the lip of the hole, holding a lit stone over it · Time: Day 1 · morning

Behind you, Bram handed the hemp to Osric at the ring, and the warden took two turns of it round his forearm and planted his boots. Bram took the pinch-bar and came down flat beside you on his belly, the bar lying alongside him, following Osric's directions. He called down to Pell that they were lifting the block, not them, and told them to say if it shifted against their leg and to pull clear once there was room.

Bram goes forward on his belly and elbows the way you did. Under his mail the crust takes his weight differently than it took yours. It gives a long dry groan deep in the timber, and white dust sifts off the rim of the hole into the light. It holds. Two lengths of a man from the rock, he is close enough now to see straight down past your outstretched arms.

You have your elbows dug into the crust and the lit chalk gripped in both hands. You breathe out slowly and the light stops shaking. It drops down the shaft clear and steady and lies on the black water. Your voice follows it.

By your light Bram finds the near edge of the block, a straight pale line under the water, and feeds the chisel lip of the bar down along it. The first time it skates off dressed stone. The second time it finds the gap where the block's edge sits on rubble, and it bites.

"Ready, Hale? Slow, together."

"Slow," Osric says from the ring.

Bram bears down. For a long moment nothing gives. Then the block lifts off the rubble a finger's width, then a hand's, and the bar bows a little under him. Behind you the hemp creaks through the old iron ring as Osric leans back on it, steady and not jerking. The line comes taut over the lip and the knots take the strain. The block turns slowly, a big squared shape rolling over on its long side through the water toward the face, the way the ring pulls. Black water heaves up round it and slaps the gallery walls. Then there's a sound under the surface, stone settling onto stone, and the bar goes light in Bram's hands.

The block is off the leg. It lies a stride away against the rubble, turned a quarter over, and the face that was hidden now faces up.

It's just under the water now, and your light falls straight on it.

You see a true circle cut deep and clean, a smooth raised disc in the middle, and straight rays running out from the disc to the ring, more than a dozen of them, evenly spaced. You know that shape. Every hospice chapel in the Lower City that took Lathander's coin had one over the door. It's the Morninglord's sun as the old temples cut it, a sunburst on a wheel. Short mason's marks run round the outside of the ring in groups. They catch your eye the way a line of handwriting does across a room, as if they're meant to be read. From up here and through moving water you can't make them out.

At the far end of the block, where it had pressed against the gallery wall, the old grey plaster has cracked as the stone rolled. A dark seam has opened there, no wider than a finger. Something behind it, deep in the gap, answers your light with a faint milky glow, like moonlight through a dirty pane. It doesn't fade the way the reflection on the water does. For a breath the lump of chalk in your hands is warmer than your own skin.

Up at the ring, Osric has seen the stone's face too. He stands very still with the hemp still wound round his forearm, and doesn't say anything about it.

"Get him up," he says. "Loop's there."

Where you are: on the white crust at the rim of the shaft, holding the lit chalk · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram, a little further along the rim, called down to Pell that the block was clear and asked whether he could get the loop under his arms. He laid the pinch-bar flat on the crust beside him and told Osric to make sure they were hauling Pell's line and not the block's. He stays spread flat at the rim, braced to steer Pell clear of the broken edge when he comes up. He told you to keep the light on Pell and said you'd look at the stone once Pell was out.

Your voice goes down the shaft, low and clear, with the loop a yard to Pell's left, under his arms and not round the leg. The light holds steady in your hands over the black water.

Osric already has the hemp in both fists. He looks along it to the lip, then at the hole, and shakes his head once. "Same line," he says, lifting the rope so Bram can see it run. Ring, loop, then Pell's knot to the silk, and the silk round the stone. If they haul now, Pell comes up with a block hung off him. He says, loud enough to carry down the shaft, that Pell must cast the silk off down there, by knot or knife, and then it will be his line.

Then you ask your quiet question about the stone. Osric doesn't answer straight away. His eyes go to the rim of the hole and the white light coming up out of it, and stay there.

"Never seen it," he says flatly. "Thirty years on this hill. Didn't know there was a face on anything down there." He shifts his grip on the hemp. "Sun's the Morninglord's. Any fool knows that much." He thinks a moment. "In Beregost they say the temple's first stones came off this hill. Before the town was a town. That's the old men talking." He tips his head toward the shaft. "Him first."

He says nothing more about the stone, and he hasn't looked at the sunburst again since it came up.

Below, under your light, the block lies a quarter-turn over in the water with its face to the roof. The finger-wide seam at its far end is still dark, but deep in it the pale something still gives back your light, dimly, and doesn't fade.

The hemp lies slack over the lip, running down to the loop at Pell's chest and the ugly knot below it. Osric keeps his boots planted at the ring with his hands on the rope and doesn't take it up. Nobody pulls until the word comes up from below.

Where you are: at the rim of the shaft, holding the light over the water · Time: Day 1 · morning

Beside you, Bram says something low and even down the shaft to Pell: the silk below the loop is still tied to the block, and he is to undo it or cut it and say when it's free. Then Bram settles flat on the crust again, hands at the lip, the pinch-bar lying along the rim. He tells the warden there is no hurry over the knot, that you all wait for Pell's word. The crust under his mail gives one more long, dry creak and goes quiet.

"Aye," Osric says. He doesn't take up an inch of hemp. He stands on the grey rock at the ring with both fists on the rope, boots planted, the turns still round his forearm.

Your arms have started to shake again. You lock your elbows into the crust and let the weight sink through your shoulders, and the light steadies. It falls white and straight down the hole onto the black water and the pale shape of the block. Your voice follows it, clear, and then you say the rest quietly, for the warden only, without turning your head.

Osric is quiet long enough that you can hear water trickling somewhere down in the gallery. "It's a stone till he's out," he says. "After that it's still under my road." He shifts his grip. The hearth is laid and the kettle full, he says, but he'll light it when Pell is on the rock, not before. He's not leaving this rope. He looks at nothing but the line.

The hemp lies slack over the lip and runs down past Bram's hands into the shaft of light. Below, the knot is still between the loop and the silk. The water stirs around Pell, and the wheel lies face-up beneath it. At the far end of the block the seam keeps its faint milky glow, steady, just where it was. Nobody up top moves. Whether the word comes, and when, is up to the man in the water.

Where you are: at the lip of the shaft, lighting it, by the ring · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram stays low on the creaking crust and calls down to Pell that you're both here. He makes no move to haul until Pell gives his signal. You say nothing and keep your eyes on the pale shape in the dark water.

Then the quiet breaks from below. There's a short wet rasp, a blade going through silk, and a slap as a slack line hits the water. Pell's voice follows, hoarse with cold and still with that bark of a laugh in it: the silk is clear, he's alone on the line, haul.

Behind you Osric leans back on the ring. The hemp comes in hand over hand, slow and even. Under your light Pell leaves the black water and walks the gallery wall up the shaft, good foot first, the bruised leg dragging after it. Chalk-water pours off him. Halfway up he starts to shake hard. Even so he gets his words out, loud enough to carry: a glass face with a glow of its own, under the road since before any of you were born. He'll not touch it, and he'll not tell Thorn.

Osric answers between pulls, flat. He didn't know there was a wall down there to be behind. Nobody's been in the third gallery in his time.

Pell's head comes up through the ragged rim beside Bram. Bram, flat on the crust, takes a fistful of wet collar and keeps the man's chest off the broken edge as the hemp drags him over. The rim crumbles under Pell's forearms and holds. Bram works backward on his elbows with him, a hand's width at a time, the crust groaning long and dry under two men's weight, until there's grey rock under both of them. Pell lies on it, dripping, pale under the chalk, shaking hard enough to rattle his teeth, and alive.

Your light still hangs over the empty hole. Pell is out of it now, so you can take it back. When you draw your arm in, the white light slides off the water, off the face of the block and the pale tag of silk knotted round it, and up the shaft wall. As it leaves, the seam at the block's far end goes dark with it. The milky glow doesn't linger or fade slowly the way warm embers would. It's there while your light touches it, and then it's gone. The gallery below goes black, and the seep keeps trickling somewhere down in it.

Your prayer gets no answer. All you have is the lump of chalk in your fist, the grey rock under your elbows when you work your way back to it, and the ache that comes into your arms the moment you let them stop holding.

Osric unwinds the hemp from his forearm, one turn and then the other, and looks down at Pell on his rock. "Glass I don't know," he says. "The low end I know a bit. Men worked long down there, they got heavy in the head. Sleepy." His jaw sets, as if he's said more than he meant to. "Fire first. Then the rest, what there is."

He goes off across the yard toward the house at his walking pace. Over his shoulder: "Kettle'll be on by the time you can walk."

Bram's pack sits where he left it on the living rock, with the case wrapped dry in its bedroll and the flap down. The pinch-bar lies along the rim of the hole on the crust. The hemp lies coiled once by the guy-ring. The sun has climbed a little. There's still a long half-day of road ahead and plenty of light to walk it.

A few breaths later, a thin grey thread of smoke goes up from the warden's chimney.

Nothing else here needs anyone this moment. The fire and whatever Osric means by "the rest" are waiting in the house, whenever the three of you want them.

Where you are: on the grey rock beside the shaft mouth, warden's yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram crouched beside Pell, remarked that he'd found himself a bath, and took his bedroll from the pack (the sealed case stayed dry inside). He wrapped it round Pell's shoulders and asked you about the leg, offering to carry Pell if it wouldn't bear weight. Then he gave Pell his shoulder and helped him toward the house over the living rock, bringing his pack and leaving the bar behind. He said wet clothes should come off by the fire first, and then Hale could tell them about his sleepy men.

You let the light go out of the chalk, tucked the warm stone into your palm, knelt, took Pell's wet sleeve and spoke to him in the soft, unhurried hospice voice. You told Bram the glass and the sunburst should wait until the case was delivered and all of you were sitting at a table, and you shook a muddy-hemmed blanket out of your roll and wrapped it over Bram's bedroll. The cold came off Pell in waves and you didn't flinch from it.

At the threshold Osric looked at the man coming in under two layers of bedding, dropped his own grey army blanket on top without a word, and went to the kettle.

That was a quarter of an hour ago. The mug by Pell's knee is empty now.

Pell said Tobin Reed's name to the fire. Then he told the warden that he'd written "drink" because the other thing had no name, and that he couldn't have told the lads to stop. Osric listened with his hands at his sides, saying neither yes nor no. When Pell finished, the warden closed the tally-book, not hard, the way you'd close a door on a sleeping room, and left his palm flat on the warped board a moment longer than he needed to.

Pell then asked three questions, and Osric answered them in order.

"Salt's always gone out. A sack or two a year to dyers in the Gate, through Tull. Since before my time." He looked at the shelf. "Her boxes, sealed, that's new. Since the thaw. One a month. Two last month. This one's the third since midsummer."

"Not a carter." He thought about it honestly. "Once. Back end of winter. Two men with a letter in Tull's hand. Walked the yard, counted the sheds. Asked how far down the water goes at the low end, and could it be pumped." His jaw shifted. "Didn't go down. I didn't offer. Good boots. They paid the carter in Amn silver for the ride up, Hob said. He bit it."

"The page." He tapped the closed book once with a knuckle. "Tull gets a fair copy every quarter. Wages, tools, deaths, all of it. Whether he reads it, ask him. Up here nobody reads."

Pell got up slowly, tried the shin and shouldered his pack. He said what he would do, and that Osric could hold him to it at the Red Sheaf: the case into Thorn's hands, the letter, her face when she reads *Vandarren*, and a careful question about what an apothecary wants with dye from a drowned gallery where men fall asleep. He added that Tobin's name was Osric's, and he'd not say it to anyone. Then he turned to Bram and you: Bram was to see to the case, you the letter, and he would walk the back again, this time where the warden says the rock is.

Osric heard that last part with his eyes on the fire, and nodded once.

At the door Pell handed the warden his own advice back with a dry edge: stay off the low end, and never go down alone.

"Nobody here to be alone with." It's nearly a joke, the first from him. It goes as soon as it came. "Leave the blanket on. Hob can bring it back."

Outside the glare is waiting. The hemp rope still lies coiled by the iron ring in the cut face, the pinch-bar lies on the crust at the rim of the hole, and a thin cold breath comes up out of the hole into the sun. The sun is still well short of noon. The track down to the Way is the one you came up, and there's half a day of road and daylight to spare.

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Pell's Word to the Warden
+ Promise: Tobin's Name Is Osric's

Where you are: outside the warden's house at the salt works, in the yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

You step out into the white glare and the door swings shut behind you on the smell of woodsmoke. You settle your pack and touch the pouch at your belt once; the letter is there, folded twice, the warden's ink stiff in the last stroke. You tell both men plainly that you go now, while the sun is well up, that you keep the letter and put it in Thorn's hand, that Bram keeps the case, and that Pell is to say the moment his leg starts lying to him. Then you fall in at Pell's side, close enough to catch him, not so close that you hover. You give the yard and the hole one short look over your shoulder.

Pell stops by the hole on the grey rock, two strides back from the bad ground. The pinch-bar lies on the white crust about ten feet past the rock's edge, too far to reach. Cold air breathes up past it out of the shaft. Pell pulls Bram's hemp back through the iron ring hand over hand, coils it over his forearm and holds it out to Bram without a word. Bram lashes it to the top of his pack, above the case.

Osric stands in his doorway, sees Pell looking at the bar, and tells him to leave it; he has a hook-pole.

Bram asks Osric to mark the broken stretch before anyone else comes up, since a cart won't hear a warning, and then for a safe way past the collapse. Osric says he will put stakes and a rope across it today. Keep to the face side, he says, a hand on the stone; the rock runs on under the dust past the hole, two strides wide, and where the spoil stops at the bend it is track on rock again all the way down. No cart will come up until there's coin, but he'll stake it anyway. He doesn't wave; he stands with his arms folded and the grey thread of his chimney rising behind him and watches you go.

Bram goes first along the cut face with a palm on the white stone, testing each step with his heel, and the ground answers with a dull solid knock. You and Pell follow in his steps. Past the bend the white spoil thins to nothing and the track is honest rock again, pale and rutted, winding down off the hill.

Once on the track, Pell talks low. He lays out the Amn silver, the two men with Tull's letter asking whether the low end could be pumped, then the boxes, one a month and then two, and the wardens' wages stopped in the same season. He starts a name, catches it, and says a cutter instead. He says he doesn't believe in that kind of luck. He agrees it waits for a table, but asks that he be the one to give Thorn the letter, so he can watch her read Vandarren before she knows you know the word. To Bram he says that if she is quick, he's to hold the case until the ninety is on the counter, then let go. You're not thieves today. Then he falls back to his usual thirty paces behind, gaze on the dust, and mutters to himself about glass, glow, sleeping men and someone wanting it pumped dry.

Bram sets a pace the bruised shin can keep, and tells Pell to speak up if it worsens, since there is no prize for arriving on his face.

The track runs down through scrub oak and gorse, over dry stream-beds, past a shepherd's fold with no shepherd in it. Pell's clothes steam, stiffen and dry, chalk cracking off at elbow and knee. The shaking leaves him in the second hour. The shin doesn't; by the third he walks like a man with one boot nailed on, but it holds.

A little after noon the track tops the last rise and the Trade Way lies below, a broad brown ribbon through pasture and hedges. Far north a smudge of forge smoke marks Beregost, a good three hours off. The sun is high and well short of turning. There's time in hand.

Bram stands on the crest, looking over country he has known for ten years. Then he stops on something, a hollow south of where the track meets the Way, about a mile off the road on the east side, with alders and a spring. From up here there is little to see: a ring of stones, rows of dark shapes inside it, and a few crows walking among them. Bram has the lead and is deciding what to do.

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: The Empty Camp in Alder Hollow

Where you are: on the crest above the Trade Way, with the party · Time: Day 1 · midday

Pell labours up the final stretch of the rise, slower than he would like, and halts a pace behind Bram, bent over with his hands braced on his knees to catch his breath. He follows Bram's gaze south, shading his eyes against the glare. He asks Bram what he has, and wants to hear what Bram thinks it is before he points. Then Pell reckons the day aloud: three hours to Beregost, four with his bad leg, and sunset about six hours off. That leaves some slack, but a detour of a mile out and a mile back costs an hour they won't get again, and they are carrying the only coin on the hill. If it's only a drover's fire, he says, they walk on. If it's an empty camp a mile from the Way, the day after the men of a quarry came down this same road, he lets the thought trail off. Then one of them should look, and he says it should be him, since he can get close unseen. He would work from the hedge line and take ten minutes at most. He won't go in alone: you would wait at the hedge, where the two of you could keep each other in sight, because the rule today is that nobody goes alone. He waits on Bram's answer.

Bram stops on the crest and points out the hollow to you and Pell. He calls it a caravan camp with a good spring and shelter under the bank, a place he has slept in himself. He says the rows down there are new, and that if anyone were using the camp there ought to be wagons. He shades his eyes and studies the shapes for movement, clothing, bedrolls or discarded harness. He says that looking properly would cost two extra miles, with Pell limping. Unless they see someone who needs help, he would keep on for Beregost and report what they've found. But he wants a look from here before anyone moves.

Bram is still for a long moment on the crest, a hand flat over his eyes against the glare, working out what the thing is before he says it.

You see what anyone could see from the rise: the ring, the rows and the crows. Nothing moves down there except the birds. No smoke, no voice carries up, and nobody calls out for help.

North, the forge smoke over Beregost stands up straight in the still air. The sun is a little past noon.

Where you are: on the crest of the rise above the hollow, beside the Way · Time: Day 1 · midday

Bram gives his report plainly, the way he would to a caravan master: beds, twenty or more, laid round the fire and left weathering for weeks. The wagons went out south. There are no wrecks and no harness lying about, and nothing to show a fight, yet nobody took their bedding along. He points at the bare grass between the hedge-end and the windbreak and says anyone in the alders could watch you cross it. He tells Pell these aren't yesterday's quarry lads, and that it isn't ten minutes on that leg. His advice is to deliver the case, report exactly what they saw, ask whether a caravan is missing, and come back by daylight on sound legs. He takes a last look at the place, then turns toward Beregost, keeping an easy pace for Pell.

Pell blinks the glare out of his eyes and says that from here he sees only crows and shapes, and that he'll take Bram's read of the rows over his own, since Bram has slept there. Then he gives the ground: the thorn hedge runs along the old ruts almost to the trees, giving cover all the way, and after it comes a hundred feet of open grass that nobody crosses unseen. His cheap version is half a mile behind the hedge to where it ends, no step onto the grass, you at the hedge where you can see both him and Bram, Bram on the crest with the case. If he sees a reason to go further he'll come back and say so first. If Bram would rather walk on, he says, he'll walk. He'd just hate to find out tomorrow that someone was alive down there at noon.

Nothing has changed in the hollow. A crow lifts, flaps a few lazy beats over the windbreak and drops again a row further on. On the Way below, a single ox-cart creaks north toward Beregost, piled with hurdles, its driver asleep on the seat with his hat over his face, the ox seeming to know the road without him. The forge smoke stands straight over the town. The sun has barely moved off noon.

Bram has already turned his shoulder toward Beregost. You are a dozen steps down the slope toward the road. Pell stands on the crest with the hedge-line below him, his weight off the bad shin.

Where you are: on the slope just below the crest, heading for the Trade Way · Time: Day 1 · midday

You turn back up the slope a dozen steps, unhurried, and say your piece: if anyone looks, all of you go, ten minutes at the hedge end, nobody out of sight, and back to the Way if it's only crows.

Pell comes down off the crest toward you, favouring the shin, and says he'll walk it. He doesn't drop back to thirty paces this time but falls in at your shoulder, close enough to catch if the leg goes. Aloud, so he'll keep it, he goes over what he's seen: twenty beds left out for weeks, the wagons gone south, nobody took their blankets. Drovers don't own twenty bedrolls, he says, and a caravan master wouldn't leave them to the weather. Then he lays out a plan: Beregost, the case, the ninety on the counter, the letter in Thorn's hand, which he asks to deliver himself if you'll let him. After that the Red Sheaf, and somewhere along the way a Fist sergeant or a priest who'll know whether a caravan is missing. Last, so it's said while he can't argue, he says that if you ever come back, the hedge end is his to walk.

Bram doesn't argue it again. He says he'd rather you all walk on, since he's seen no sign of anyone alive and that isn't enough to send a man down on a bad leg. He goes down the last of the slope onto the Way and waits on the verge.

The ox-cart is ahead of you on the brown road, going north at the speed of an animal that has decided the whole day is its own. It's a two-wheeled thing, piled shoulder-high with woven hazel hurdles roped down in a stack. The driver is asleep on the seat with his hat over his face, one boot up on the shaft.

Staying well clear of the ox, Bram calls out in his road voice: "Ho, driver!"

The ox stops dead.

The driver sways forward with the jolt, catches himself on the seat-rail and pushes his hat up. He's an old man, brown as a saddle, with white stubble and pale eyes creased from squinting at fields. He looks at the ox first, as if it owes him an explanation. Then he looks at Bram, the mail and the shield, and his shoulders go stiff for a moment before he takes in the limping man in a grey blanket and you beside him.

Bram asks whether there's room for a hurt-legged man to ride.

"Seat's mine." The old man sniffs and jerks a thumb back at the stack. "Tail's free. Room on the tailboard for one, if he keeps a hand on them hurdles over the ruts. Lose me one in the ditch and he walks." He looks Pell over, chalk-white to the collar. "Fell in a lime pit, did you, lad?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. Bram asks about the hollow and the bedding, and the old man's face changes. He doesn't look toward the hollow. He looks the other way, north up the road.

"Don't go off the road. Not me." He scratches his jaw. "Sleep on the seat, I do, and Bess there knows the way home." The ox flicks an ear. "But there's talk. Wagons going south and not getting to Nashkel. Three this year, or four, depends who's buying. My brother says it's gnolls down out of the hills, carrying folk off." He shrugs, as if his brother says a lot of things. "There's a notice at the Jovial Juggler in Beregost. Fist put it up, market day before last. A woman sergeant, Kell. Coin for any word on lost wagons, it says. Somebody read it out." He settles his hat. "So that's your somebody, if you've a tale. Not me. I make hurdles."

He gathers up the reins, though Bess plainly doesn't need them.

"Wick," he adds. "Dunstan Wick. Beregost by mid-afternoon at her pace. Getting on, or not?"

The tailboard stands empty behind the hurdles, about knee-high. The forge smoke over Beregost stands straight up in the north, and the sun has barely moved past noon.

Where you are: on the Way beside the ox-cart · Time: Day 1 · midday

The session is over.

Sefa slows as the silence settles over the yard, one hand drifting to the book at her belt without quite touching it. She glances to Pell and Bram.

"That must be the warden, but a whole quarry gone still? No mules, no men, just him watching us." She keeps her voice low. "I'll say a word to him from here. If I'm wrong, we've lost nothing. If you see anything move behind those sheds, sing out."

She steps forward a few paces, not enough to close the distance, and raises a hand in greeting that could be friendly or a signal to stop.

"Morning!" she calls, clear and even. "Maela Thorn sent us from Beregost. We're expected — for a case of dye-salts from the warden. Is that you?"

Sefa keeps her hands open at her sides, meeting the warden's eyes without challenge.

"She paid us, Warden — ninety gold to walk the road and carry the case, and not one coin of it until it's in her shop by sunset. That's the whole of what we know. If your men's wages have gone missing, we hadn't heard a word of it until now."

The table was well met. The session held a good, steady tension — a quiet quarry with missing men, a warden with more on his mind than the case, and a hole that opened under one of us at the worst moment. The world felt lived-in: Osric not a quest-giver but a man up to his knees in old stone and unpaid wages, with boundaries and a weary kind of care.

The play worked for me too. The party talked like three hired hands who know enough to be wary but not enough to run. Bram read the hollow like a carter, Pell thought like a man who’s used to getting close unseen, and Sefa kept finding the only work she can do — steady the light, steady the living, say the prayer and keep it short.

I never felt shoved toward any of it. The mystery stayed in the margins: the sunburst, the seam that answered light, Thorn's boxes and the Amn silver, a caravan camp left to the crows. The session ended before sunset and before the case left our hands, which is exactly where it should have. The table has a real momentum now.

Until next we light a stone.

Pell's player struck me as the careful one — the kind who hoards information, asks the questions the scene doesn't volunteer, and wants to deliver the letter himself because he knows the best moment to watch a face is when it reads a name it didn't expect. screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)
Saves: Dexterity saving throw +6 (proficient); Intelligence saving throw +4 (proficient); Strength saving throw +0; Constitution saving throw +1; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +1
Attacks: Shortsword +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing; Dagger +6 to hit, 1d4+3 piercing, thrown 20/60; Shortbow +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 80/320; Sneak Attack: +3d6 once a turn with advantage or an ally beside the target
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Sneak Attack 3d6; Cunning Action: Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action; Uncanny Dodge: a reaction halves the damage of an attack he can see; Fast Hands (Thief): a bonus action to use an object — a potion on another, a lock, a lamp; Second-Story Work: climbs at full speed; Thieves' Cant
Limits: Light armour; 33 hit points — he cannot stand at the front for long; Sneak Attack needs advantage or an ally beside the target
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 31 gp; 2 ep; 6 sp; 55 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Thieves' Tools; Main hand: Shortsword
Pack: Arrow ×20; Bedroll and Rations; Dagger ×2; Flask of Oil ×2; Hooded Lantern; Potion of Healing ×3; Shortbow; Silk Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram takes the front of the track at an easy pace, shield held low, while Sefa keeps a few steps back between you both. You drift to one side and read the yard the way you'd read a merchant's back wall.

Bram says quietly that it's quiet for a working quarry. He walks up to the house, sword sheathed, and stops a few paces short of the man in the doorway to give him room. He gives his name, says Maela Thorn sent the three of you for her sealed case of dye-salts, and asks whether the man is the warden. He glances back at the abandoned cart and asks if everyone stopped for something.

Sefa slows, one hand near the book at her belt. She remarks, low, that a whole quarry gone still is strange, with no mules or men and only the one man watching. She steps forward a few paces, keeping her distance, and raises a hand that could be a greeting or a signal to stop. She calls out that Maela Thorn sent you from Beregost, that you're expected, and asks whether he is the warden with the dye-salts.

Close up, the quarry is just as quiet. White dust lies over everything in a soft skin, and it keeps every mark made on it. You go over the ground near the lower cut, the shadow under the lifting frame, and the stretch between the sheds and the cart.

Pell has already read the opening of this scene, so this continues from there.

You see it well enough. Nobody was dragged off anywhere. There's no blood, no scuffle, no furrow of heels in the dust. A crowd of boot prints, a dozen men or a few more, heads down the cart track the way the three of you just came. The strides are short and even, overlapping, the tracks of men walking together and in no hurry. One set of mule hooves goes with them, led on a short line. The edges of the prints have gone soft under a night's settling dust. They were made yesterday, not this morning.

The tools aren't scattered either. Seen from this angle, the hammers by the lower cut lie in a row along a squared block, heads together. The wedges are stacked beside them and every handle points at the warden's house. The cart's traces were unbuckled, not cut. Someone laid all this out on purpose, the way you'd put a key on a table before walking out a door.

The man in the doorway lets you come. Bram stops a few paces off, Sefa's call carries across the yard, and your easy question lands last. The warden looks at each of you in turn, the big one first. Up close he's in his fifties, grey-bearded, with white dust in the creases of his knuckles and his apron. The keys at his belt are old iron, a dozen of them.

"Hale. Osric Hale. I'm the warden." His voice is gravel, and he uses no more of it than he has to. He tips his chin at the cart. "They stopped for pay. Noon bell, yesterday. Three weeks of none, and they walked." He doesn't sound angry about it. "I'd have walked too, if it was my back."

Then he looks at Sefa, because she named the salts. "The case is inside. Sealed, like she wants it." He doesn't step out of the doorway. "Thorn's bought it. So she's paid someone. Not me, and not them." He nods at the empty track. "Before it leaves my house, I'll hear who she paid. And whether she knows where my men's wages went."

He waits with his arms folded, his eyes on Bram, as if the big man in mail is the one who'll answer for all three.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, near the warden's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram had spoken first, agreeing with the warden that a wage gone unpaid for three weeks is a fair reason to down tools. He kept his hands well clear of his sword, pointed out that you are hired carriers who were never told who took Thorn's money, and asked who handles wages and who sold her the salts. He offered to carry a tally or letter but promised no answer.

Sefa, hands open, told the warden that Thorn pays ninety gold for the walk and the carrying, nothing until the case is in her shop by sunset, and that you knew nothing of missing wages. She offered to take what's under the seal and carry his complaint back, or, if he keeps you, Thorn will say the case never came and owe you nothing.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving. Watching his face, you find little to puzzle over. His hands stay folded and never go near the keys. When Sefa speaks of keeping you here, his jaw shifts, the look of a man told something he already knew. This isn't a man playing for leverage. He's spent three weeks writing letters, and you are the first people up the track to give him a straight answer. Once, when you spoke of the only coin on the hill, his eyes go past you toward the lower cut and come straight back.

"House Vandarren," Osric says. "Patriars, in the Gate. Whitestone's theirs on paper. Their factor's a man called Tull, in the Lower City. Coin comes up from Tull, I pay the lads. He tells Bram the salts weren't sold by him: he cuts it, boxes it, seals it, and it goes. Somebody paid for it, and that's Tull, so that's Vandarren. Fourteen men are owed three weeks, fifty-odd gold, the carter most. They're in Beregost now, drinking what they had left. Not taken, not run off. Walked. They'll tell anyone who stands them a round.

Osric stays standing. The case goes with you, he says, and a letter to Thorn with it; she can ask Tull where the rest went. He looks at the crossed-out lines, then at Sefa. "I cut stone. I don't write much." He pushes the pen an inch toward her. "You write a fair hand?"

The case sits on the table between you all, untouched.

Osric answers your offer with a short nod and nothing more. To Bram's parting words he says "Always do," and he takes his place in the doorway again, arms folded, to watch you go.

This is your trade, and the dust makes it easy. Below the yard the track runs along the lip of the lower cut, a wide shelf of packed white spoil with the drop on the left. You can see it plainly enough: a rope round the block, the beam under its edge, two people above pulling and prying, and it would roll off your leg in a few minutes. Alone, with no purchase, it's a long hard fight.

Your narration of this is yours; what follows is what the others did and what the world did in answer.

Bram and Sefa are with you across the yard. Bram takes the end of the hemp loop you hold out, and whoever is nearest hauls you upright. Nobody answers your thanks with more than that. They do not argue with the round at the Red Sheaf, nor with the one for Hob Carrow.

On the way across the yard you say your piece low, before the house: the carved sun-wheel with its tallies, the glass face behind the plaster glowing by itself, the men who got heavy in the head, and the salt growing on the same walls. Osric Hale looks down at the white puddle spreading from your boots, then at you, and says nothing about it. He takes the blanket off the cot, a grey army thing gone thin at the folds, and drops it over your shoulders as you crouch at the hearth. You ask your question, without any edge, and you tell the others you'll take a quarter of an hour and then you walk.

Hale doesn't sit down. He stands by the table where the case used to be and looks at the fire instead of at you.

"Heavy in the head. That's how they said it." He gives it one fact at a time. "Sit down on the ledge for a breather, wake up with the lamp guttered. Didn't know they'd gone." A pause. "Worse the longer you stayed down. So I put them on short turns. An hour down, an hour up. Nobody alone."

He's quiet for a moment. The fire cracks.

*Tobin Reed, cutter. Found in the low cut end of shift. Drink, in four feet of water.*

"Three years back," Hale says. "Scraping salt, end of the day, on his own. I found him face down." He looks at the line he wrote and not at you. "That's what I put."

He leaves the book open and says nothing more. He doesn't say Tobin drank, and he doesn't say he didn't. He stands with his hands at his sides and the fire on one side of his face, and lets the page say what it says.

The water steams in the mug by your knee. Feeling is coming back into your fingers in hot, needling waves. The quarter of an hour you asked for is yours, and the sun outside is still well short of noon.

She takes the place at your side, close enough to catch you, not close enough to hover, and gives the yard and the hole one short look back.

You stop by the hole on the grey rock, two strides back from the bad ground. The pinch-bar lies on the white crust about ten feet past the rock's edge, too far to reach, and cold air breathes up past it from the shaft. You pull the hemp back through the iron ring hand over hand, wet and gritty, coil it over your forearm and hold it out to Bram without a word. He takes it and lashes it to the top of his pack, above the case.

Osric, back in his doorway, sees you looking at the bar and tells you to leave it; he has a hook-pole.

Bram tells Osric to mark the broken stretch before anyone else comes up, since a cart won't hear a warning, and then asks for a safe way past the collapse. Osric says stakes and a rope across it today. Keep to the face side, hand on the stone; the rock runs on under the dust past the hole, two strides wide, and where the spoil stops at the bend it's track on rock again all the way down. No cart comes up till there's coin, but he'll stake it. He doesn't wave; he stands arms folded, chimney smoke rising behind him, and watches you go.

Bram goes first along the cut face with a palm on the white stone, testing each step with his heel, and the ground answers with a dull solid knock. Sefa and you follow in his steps. Past the bend the white spoil thins to nothing and the track is honest rock again, winding down off the hill.

Once on the track proper, you lay it out low for the other two: the Amn silver, the two men with Tull's letter, the boxes, the wardens' wages stopped. You start a name, catch it, say a cutter instead. You ask to be the one who hands Thorn the letter, and tell Bram to keep hold of the case until the ninety is on the counter. Then you drop back to your thirty paces, eyes on the dust, the grey blanket pulled tight over your straps.

Bram sets a pace your bruised shin can keep, and tells you to say so if it worsens; there's no prize for arriving on your face.

The track runs down through scrub oak and gorse, over dry stream-beds, past a shepherd's fold with no shepherd in it. Your clothes steam, stiffen and dry, chalk cracking off at elbows and knees. The shaking leaves you in the second hour. The shin doesn't; by the third you walk like a man with one boot nailed on, but it holds, every step.

A little after noon the track tops the last rise and the Trade Way lies below, a broad brown ribbon through pasture and hedges. Far north a smudge of forge smoke marks Beregost, a good three hours off at this pace. The sun is high and well short of turning. There's time in hand.

Bram stands on the crest, looking the country over, then stops on something to the south, a hollow a mile off the road with alders and a spring. You can't make out much from where you stand. He has the lead.

Conditions: Bruised shin (not broken), Stiff shin, limping

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: The Empty Camp in Alder Hollow

Where you are: on the crest above the Trade Way, with the party · Time: Day 1 · midday

Bram stops on the crest and points out the hollow to you and Sefa. He calls it a caravan camp with a good spring and shelter under the bank, a place he has slept in himself. He says the rows down there are new, and that if anyone were using the camp there ought to be wagons. He shades his eyes and studies the shapes for movement, clothing, bedrolls or discarded harness. He says that looking properly would cost two miles, with your leg as it is. Unless they see someone who needs help, he would keep on for Beregost and report what they've found. But he wants a look from here before anyone moves.

Sefa comes up level with him and follows his gaze. She asks Bram, in a low voice, what he has seen. She says the rows and the ring of stones could be drovers or what is left of them, and asks whether to look or to keep to the Way and tell the Fist or the temple. She glances back toward you. She says she has light and a steady hand for the dead if that's what lies below, but she won't walk the party into an ambush for a look.

Bram is still for a long moment on the crest, working out what the thing is before he says it.

Bram is still for a long moment on the crest, a hand flat over his eyes against the glare. He's working out what the thing is before he says it, the way you asked him to.

He reads it the way he'd read any camp he was riding into. His eyes find a detail a mile off and hold it. He says nothing yet, but his gaze settles on the hollow and stays there.

You shade your eyes and look hard, and the glare beats you. The pasture swims white-green, the alders are a dark smudge, and the rows are only shapes with crows among them. From here you can't tell one thing from another.

The ground between here and the hollow is another matter. That's your trade, and you read it without trying. A hawthorn hedge follows the old ruts down from the Way almost to the alders, a little higher than a man, and solid enough to walk behind unseen from the spring. Where the hedge stops there's about a hundred feet of open grass before the windbreak, and no cover on it at all. The alders are thick round the spring. Anyone sitting in them could watch the whole of that hundred feet, and nobody on the grass could see in.

Sefa, beside Bram, sees what anyone could see from the rise: the ring, the rows and the crows. Nothing moves down there except the birds. No smoke, no voice carries up, and nobody calls out for help.

North, the forge smoke over Beregost stands up straight in the still air. The sun is a little past noon.

Where you are: on the crest of the rise above the hollow, beside the Way · Time: Day 1 · midday

Bram speaks plainly, the way he'd report to a caravan master: beds, twenty or more, set round the fire and left to weather for weeks. The wagons went out south, and there are no wrecks, no harness strewn about, nothing to show a fight, yet nobody took their bedding. He points at the bare grass between the hedge-end and the windbreak and says anyone in the alders could watch you cross it. He tells you these aren't yesterday's quarry lads, and that it isn't ten minutes on that leg. His advice is to deliver the case, report exactly what they saw, ask whether a caravan is missing, and come back by daylight on sound legs. He takes a last look at the place, then turns toward Beregost, keeping an easy pace for you.

Sefa keeps a step back from the crest edge and reads the same things: no smoke, nothing moving, no voice, only crows. She says that if someone down there were calling for help they'd have heard it, and that no one carries a warning faster by arriving dead or limping after sunset. She says you may take your look at the hedge if your leg allows it, provided you stay within her sight, but unless you find someone alive you touch nothing and don't linger. She sides with Bram on telling the right ear in town. Then she settles her pack and starts down toward the road, saying they'll wait on the Way, not on the hill, and that if a crow lifts differently you should hurry back, as fast as the shin lets you.

Nothing has changed in the hollow. A crow lifts, flaps a few lazy beats over the windbreak and drops again a row further on. On the Way below, a single ox-cart creaks north toward Beregost, piled with hurdles, its driver asleep on the seat with his hat over his face, the ox seeming to know the road without him. The forge smoke stands straight over the town. The sun has barely moved off noon.

Bram has already turned his shoulder toward Beregost. Sefa is a dozen steps down the slope toward the road. You stand on the crest with the hedge-line below you and your weight off the bad shin.

Where you are: on the crest, above the hedge-line · Time: Day 1 · midday

You come down off the crest after Sefa, who had turned back up the slope to say her piece: if anyone looks, you all go, ten minutes at the hedge end, nobody out of sight, and back to the Way if it's only crows. You fall in at her shoulder and say your plan aloud.

Bram doesn't argue it again. He says he'd rather you all walk on, since he's seen no sign of anyone alive and that alone doesn't justify sending you down on a bad leg. He goes down the last of the slope onto the Way and waits on the verge.

The ox-cart is ahead of you on the brown road, going north at the speed of an animal that has decided the whole day is its own. It's a two-wheeled thing, piled shoulder-high with woven hazel hurdles roped down in a stack. The driver is asleep on the seat with his hat over his face, one boot up on the shaft.

Staying well clear of the ox, Bram calls out in his road voice: "Ho, driver!"

The ox stops dead.

The driver sways forward with the jolt, catches himself on the seat-rail and pushes his hat up. He's an old man, brown as a saddle, with white stubble and pale eyes creased from squinting at fields. He looks at the ox first, as if it owes him an explanation. Then he looks at Bram, the mail and the shield, and his shoulders go stiff for a moment before he takes in you in your grey blanket, limping, and Sefa beside you.

Bram asks whether he could spare a place for a man with a hurt leg.

"Seat's mine." The old man sniffs and jerks a thumb back at the stack. "Tail's free. Room on the tailboard for one, if he keeps a hand on them hurdles over the ruts. Lose me one in the ditch and he walks." He looks you over, chalk-white to the collar. "Fell in a lime pit, did you, lad?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. Bram asks about the hollow and the bedding, and the old man's face changes. He doesn't look toward the hollow. He looks the other way, north up the road.

"Don't go off the road. Not me." He scratches his jaw. "Sleep on the seat, I do, and Bess there knows the way home." The ox flicks an ear. "But there's talk. Wagons going south and not getting to Nashkel. Three this year, or four, depends who's buying. My brother says it's gnolls down out of the hills, carrying folk off." He shrugs, as if his brother says a lot of things. "There's a notice at the Jovial Juggler in Beregost. Fist put it up, market day before last. A woman sergeant, Kell. Coin for any word on lost wagons, it says. Somebody read it out." He settles his hat. "So that's your somebody, if you've a tale. Not me. I make hurdles."

He gathers up the reins, though Bess plainly doesn't need them.

"Wick," he adds. "Dunstan Wick. Beregost by mid-afternoon at her pace. Getting on, or not?"

The tailboard stands empty behind the hurdles, about knee-high, for whoever wants it. The forge smoke over Beregost stands straight up in the north, and the sun has barely moved past noon.

Pell, the tailboard's being offered to you.

Where you are: on the Way beside the ox-cart · Time: Day 1 · midday

The session is over.
